en: CHAPTER 1 <1.1> || Homage to Gaṇeśa.

O wise ones, listen: for the sake of enlightening those scholars among whom there are many diverse disputes concerning the statements of Manu and others on various matters, this *Dāyabhāga* (the law of inheritance) shall be examined.

<1.2> Now, the division of inheritance (*dāyabhāga*) is defined. Regarding this, Nārada says: "Where the division of paternal property is arranged by the sons, that is declared by the learned to be the title of dispute known as *dāyabhāga*. [N 13.1]

<1.3> That which has come from the father is "paternal" (*pitryam*). And that is said to be the ownership (*svatva*) arising upon the death of the father. Both terms—"of the paternal property" (*pitryasya*) and "by the sons" (*putraiḥ*)—are indicative of any relative whatsoever; for the term "division of inheritance" (*dāyabhāga*) is applied even when there is a division of the wealth of any relative by any relative. For this very reason, Nārada, having introduced the title of law "Division of Inheritance," also demonstrated the division of the wealth of the mother and others. Likewise, Manu also, without employing terms such as "father" and so forth, stated: "This dharma pertaining to pleasure between husband and wife has been declared to you..."

Having begun with the words, "In times of distress, the acquisition of offspring, and the division of inheritance—learn [this]" (M 9.103), [the author] has explained everything up to the division of the wealth of relatives.

The word *dāya* is derived from the sense "that which is given" (*dīyate*). Furthermore, the use of the verb *dadāti* ("to give") is figurative, because the result is the same: the cessation of the former owner's ownership and the subsequent arising of another's ownership, as occurs when one dies or renounces the world. However, there is no act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) by the deceased or others in that case. Consequently, the term *dāya* is conventionally established for any property upon the death of the previous owner where ownership was dependent upon that prior connection.

<1.6> Now, is the division (*vibhāga*) of the inheritance (*dāya*) the state of having divided parts, or is it the state of being disconnected from the inheritance? It cannot be the former, because that would entail the destruction of the inheritance. Nor can it be the second, because even in the case of something that is connected [to another], one uses such expressions as, "This property of my brother is not divided from me."

Nor should it be said that "partition" (*vibhāga*) is the determination of ownership—arising from the entire estate of all [co-heirs]—with respect to specific objects, on the grounds that their relationship [to the estate] is indistinguishable. This is because a relationship that is counteracted by the existence of other related parties can only produce ownership manifested by partition with respect to the individual parts. Furthermore, it would involve the conceptual complexity of postulating the simultaneous production and destruction of ownership over the father’s entire estate; moreover, it would be useless, as there would be no resulting capacity for disposal according to one's will.

It is said: Partition (*vibhāga*) is the manifestation of ownership that has arisen over land, gold, and so forth belonging to a single location—which, due to the absence of a definitive means of proof (*vinigamanā-pramāṇa*), is unsettled and unfit for specific Vaiśeṣika transactions—by means of the casting of lots (*guṭikā-pāta*) and other such methods. Alternatively, partition is the specific allocation (*viśeṣeṇa bhajana*) or the making known of ownership.

Furthermore, even in cases where a single slave girl, cow, or similar object is held in common by many, ownership is manifested there as well through the results of carrying, milking, and so forth, at their respective times. Thus Bṛhaspati says:

One should employ a single woman for the work in each house according to her share. Just as water from a well or a pond is drawn out and taken in accordance with need, so too should that [work] be divided by means of skillful methods; otherwise, it will become useless.
These three half-verses are located in various places and are not sequential.
[Objection:
"When the father has passed away, the sons shall divide the father's wealth. [N 13.2ab]

Based on this statement by Nārada, "they shall divide the father’s wealth," the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) implies that sons have no ownership (*svatva*) therein prior to partition. Nor does partition constitute the cause of ownership, for that would lead to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of ownership even over the property of one who is not a relative. It is replied: Because of the common usage, "this is ours" immediately after the death of the father or others, and because ownership is accepted even in the case of an only son without a formal partition, the death of the relative alone is the cause of ownership; therefore, there is no over-extension.

<1.13> Now, acquisition (*arjana*) is indeed the activity of the acquirer, and the status of ownership depends upon that acquisition. Therefore, it is logical that for a son, birth itself constitutes acquisition; hence, the sons' ownership over [the property] exists while the father is still living, and not from his death. For this very reason it has been said: "In some cases, birth itself [constitutes ownership], as in the case of paternal wealth.
<1.14> This is not so, because it contradicts Manu and others. Thus says Manu:
"After both the father and the mother [have died], the brothers, having assembled, [should divide] equally..."

"They shall divide the paternal inheritance, for they have no ownership while [the parents] are alive" (M 9.104). In response to the objection—namely, why there is no division of property among sons even when their parents are living—the answer is given: "because at that time they lack ownership.

Nor should it be said that this statement intends to express a lack of independence, as in the case of the verse beginning "the wife and the son," because there is no evidence for such ownership at that time. However, in the case of the wife and others, since ownership is established by the fact that "whatever they acquire or earn belongs to them," it is appropriate to describe their lack of independence.

<1.17> Furthermore, even if they lack ownership over what has been acquired by themselves, there would be a contradiction with the Śruti, because it would result in the cessation of Vedic rites that must be accomplished by means of one's own wealth. <1.18> And Devala clarifies that they indeed have no ownership over the paternal estate, as follows: "When the father has passed away, the sons shall divide the father’s wealth."

For these sons would lack ownership while their faultless father remains alive. Furthermore, even if sons possessed ownership over the paternal wealth while the father was still living, there would be a partition against the father’s will.

Moreover, there is no authoritative evidence for the claim that ownership arises from birth alone, since birth is not recorded in the legal treatises (*smṛti*) as being of the nature of acquisition (*arjana*). In some places, the phrase "birth alone" is merely an indirect description, because the relationship between father and son is based on birth, and the father’s death is the cause of [the son's] ownership.

<1.21> It is not contradictory that the ownership of one thing arises through the activity of another, because this is rooted in the sacred scriptures (śāstra). This is also observed in the world: for in the act of giving, the ownership of the recipient over the object arises solely from the donor’s action of relinquishing it while specifying a particular intended recipient.

Ownership does not arise from acceptance, for if it did, the one who accepts would necessarily become the giver; indeed, the nature of an act as "giving" consists in the result of transferring ownership to another, and that result depends upon the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). For just as a sacrificer (*yajamāna*), even while performing the renunciation of an object with a deity in view, is not called the "offerer" (*hotṛ*), but rather only the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) who performs the casting of that very renunciation into the fire is called the "offerer"—so too should it be here. Furthermore, in scriptural injunctions such as "having mentally designated the recipient," the term "giving" (*dāna*) is observed to apply even prior to acceptance.

<1.23> But surely, "acceptance" (*grahaṇa*) means taking possession (*svīkāra*), because of the use of the suffix * cvi* to denote the transformation of something into its opposite (e.g., *abhūtatadbhāve cvipratyayaḥ*). Taking possession is an activity consisting in making what is not one's own into one's own. How, then, can there be ownership even prior to that? <1.24> It is said in reply: although ownership has already arisen, it is made fit for use according to one's will by the activity of the recipient through the cognition "this is mine. This is the meaning of the word "acceptance" (*svīkāra*).

Furthermore, because of its association with officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) and teaching (*adhyāpana*), the act of receiving gifts (*pratigraha*)—even if it does not produce ownership—is not contradictory to being a form of acquisition (*arjana*), since ownership arises only from the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in the case of officiating and so forth.
<1.25> Furthermore, the very act of the son’s living at the time of his father’s death would constitute his acquisition [of property].

Moreover, regarding the wealth of a brother or others, one must—whether unwillingly or not—admit that ownership for another brother arises either from the [first] brother’s death or from the living at the time of that death.

<1.26> Therefore, the passage beginning with "after this, of the father" (*ata ūrdhvaṃ pituś ca*) is intended to indicate the ownership existing at that specific time; it merely restates the partition obtained by choice at that very moment, because since it is already established, a formal injunction (*vidhi*) is untenable.

Nor is a restrictive rule possible—such as "they may live together or separately out of a desire for dharma" (Manu 9.111ab)—because that would contradict Manu. Furthermore, since partition has a visible purpose, neither a restriction on its performance nor a restriction on its timing is possible. Moreover, the phrase "when the father has passed away" implies that partition should occur immediately thereafter and not later; for there is no contradiction here comparable to the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice (which occurs upon the birth of a son despite the death of the child), and because the period from the father's death until the end of one's life is obtained solely through one's own will.

<1.29> Therefore, the statement of Manu must be explained as being intended to prohibit partition among sons even when the father is alive, despite their [theoretical] ownership. However, that would be unjust, as it would result in the text losing its own literal meaning. <31.0> Consequently, the statement of Manu and others is for the purpose of making it known that ownership over that wealth does not exist while both parents are living, but rather only when they have passed away; one [interpretation] is literal (*śābda*), while the other is based on the underlying sense (*ārtha*). <1.31> Nor is mere death alone intended to be expressed; rather, it indicates [other states] such as being an outcast (*patita*) or having renounced the world (*pravrajita*), because these share the same quality of being causes for the destruction of ownership (*svatva*). <1.32> Thus says Nārada:
When the mother’s menses have ceased, when sisters have been given away in marriage, or when the father has perished, is without refuge, or has passed away and is free from desire;

[N 13.3] <1.33> "perished" means deceased; "without refuge" means devoid of the householder stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*). When there is the reading *nivṛtte vāpi maraṇāt*, it then means "having returned from death," i.e., while he is still living and free from desire; as for the alternative reading *nispṛhe*, it lacks authoritative support.

<1.34> Here too, because it is made known that sons acquire ownership over their father’s wealth through such factors as the cessation of desire [for other acquisitions], this one time for partition—which is obtained through mere wish—is restated; for a restatement follows what has already been established, and that establishment arises from ownership. <1.35> Since even a single person possesses ownership over his own wealth, partition could be obtained by the wish of one alone; therefore, the state of being "assembled" (*sametya*)—which implies association—is restated as something already possible under one alternative view. Otherwise, since plurality would also be understood [from the word *sametya*], there would be no partition between two people at all, due to the absence of a scriptural rule prescribing partition for two.
<1.36> But surely, when the father has passed away, the eldest alone is entitled to the property, not the others. As Manu says:
"The eldest alone shall take the paternal wealth in its entirety;
the rest shall depend upon him, just as they did upon their father. [M 9.105]
In this context, the "eldest" (jyeṣṭha) is intended as one who averts the hell named Put, and not merely with respect to being the first-born while the father is still alive. As Manu says:
"By the mere birth of an eldest son, a man becomes a possessor of a son and is freed from his debt to the ancestors; therefore, he [the eldest] deserves to receive [the inheritance]. (9.106)
"He alone is the son born of dharma by whom one pays off debts and through whom one attains infinity; others they know as born of desire.
[M 9.107] This is not so, because of the scriptural teaching that the eldest brother's authority is dependent on the will of all. As Nārada says:
The eldest brother should support all his younger brothers who desire it, just as a father does;

or a capable younger brother may do so, for the stability of the family depends upon capability. Thus, even a younger brother, being capable, may support them by his own will; therefore, seniority is not the sole determining factor. As Manu says:
Thus they may dwell together or separately out of a desire for dharma;
dharma increases when they are separate, therefore separation is in accordance with dharma.
By the two words "together" or "separately," and by the word "out of a desire," he shows that this is optional according to one's wish.

<1.38> Thus, there are two times: one is when the father’s ownership has ceased, and the other is when the father’s ownership has not yet ceased, occurring by the father’s own will. <1.39> It is not the case that there are three times to be observed—namely, first when the father has passed away; second, when the father’s desire [for the son] has ceased and the mother’s menses have also ceased; and third, when the mother’s menses have not ceased but the father’s desire has ceased, occurring by his will. For if the cessation of the mother’s menses were merely a qualification of the father’s cessation of desire, [the distinction would be redundant].

"A thirty-year-old man should marry a pleasing twelve-year-old girl, or a twenty-four-year-old man an eight-year-old girl, lest he fall away from dharma," because of this injunction by Manu regarding the time for marriage; and because of the injunction regarding the time for proceeding to another stage of life, "one should go to the forest at fifty"; and because, at that time, since menstruation has ceased, if the mother is no longer available and the father has lost interest in worldly affairs or retired to the forest-hermitage (vānaprastha), there would follow the undesirable consequence of non-partition even if the sons themselves so desire.

<1.40> If it is argued that the time for the division of paternal property is simply the state of having ceased desire, without further qualification, we say no; for there would follow the undesirable consequence that even if the father has fallen from his caste (*patita*), there could be no division as long as his desire has not ceased. <1.41> If one were to assert that this too is another [time for division], it would result in a fourfold set of times: the death of the father, his falling from caste, his cessation of desire, and his [expressed] wish.

<1.42> As for the statement that sons have independence regarding partition when their father is incapable of performing his duties, that is due to ignorance of the authoritative texts. Thus says Hārīta: "While the father lives, sons have no independence in the acquisition, expenditure, or protection of wealth. At will, however, the eldest son may attend to the affairs of wealth if the father is impoverished, away on a journey, or afflicted by illness. [H 4.1, 3] Śaṅkha and Likhita have stated very clearly: "If the father is incapable, the eldest son, or the next in order who understands the business and is authorized by him, shall manage the family affairs; but there is no division of inheritance against the father’s will. If he is aged, mentally deranged, or chronically ill, the eldest alone shall protect the assets like a father for the others. For the family is rooted in the inheritance; those with a father are not independent, and the same applies when the mother is in such a state. [ŚL 270] <1.43> These two statements, having prohibited partition when the father is incapable of performing his duties or is chronically ill, declare that the eldest son—or the next younger brother who understands the business—shall manage the household. Therefore, the phrase "but not against the father’s will" refers precisely to this. The notion that there is a division of inheritance while the father is incapable of performing his duties is a mere scribal error.

<1.44> Therefore, there are only two appropriate times for the cessation of ownership: one through [the father's] becoming an outcaste, loss of desire, or death; and another while ownership still exists, by his own will.

<1.45> As for the statement "when the mother’s menses have ceased," this refers to the property of the grandfather and others, because when the menses have ceased, there is no possibility of the birth of other sons. Even then, the partition among sons occurs only by the will of the father. For if a partition of the inherited wealth were made while the menses have not yet ceased, it would result in the loss of livelihood for those born later. And that is not proper.
For it is said: "Those who have been born, those yet to be born, and those dwelling in the womb—all of them desire a livelihood; the deprivation of a livelihood is censured. [Vy 253]

<1.46> Precisely because there are two points in time regarding the paternal estate, Manu, Gautama, and others have used the word *ūrdhvam* (afterwards) instead of *mṛte* (upon death), as in the phrase *ūrdhvam pituḥ* (after the father [has died]), since at that point the father’s ownership has ceased. It is for this very purpose that *ūrdhvam* was stated. Thus, this is one time for partition. By the rule *ūrdhvam vibhāgāj jātas tu* (but one born after partition), another time for partition is shown by the father’s own will when he still possesses a desire [for his sons]. <1.47> As for the phrase *dattāsu bhaginīṣu ca* (and when the sisters have been given away), it does not serve to define a specific time, but rather to ensure that they must necessarily be given [in marriage]. Likewise—
"Whatever remains from the paternal inheritance after the father's debt has been paid from it,

that is to be divided by the brothers so that the father does not remain a debtor. This statement of Nārada is intended to establish the necessity of clearing the father's debt, not to designate the time for partition.

From this statement of Nārada, the following point is established: the debt of the father and others must be divided or cleared off by the partitioners only with the consent of the creditor (*uttamarṇa*), because the purpose of that [statement] is precisely to demonstrate the division of the wealth remaining after such clearance.
For this very reason, Yājñavalkya also declares the division of the mother’s property to be only of that which remains after debts:
"The daughters [inherit] the remainder from the mother's debt; in their absence, the lineage. (YDh 2.117cd)
This will be explained in detail under the section on the recovery of debts (*ṛṇādāna*).

Alternatively, when the sisters have been given [in marriage], the mother’s property must be divided by the sons alone; as long as they have not been given, it remains common property shared with them. This point shall be discussed at its proper occasion. Thus far, two occasions for the partition of the father’s property have been stated.
CHAPTER 2 <2.1> Now the time for the partition of the estate of the grandfather and others is declared. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"The partition [of the estate] among brothers has been demonstrated to take place upon the absence of both parents."
[The partition of inheritance] is recommended even while the parents are alive, provided the mother’s menses have ceased (nivṛtte rajasi).

This statement does not concern the father’s property, because that would render the rule "but one born after partition" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.122) devoid of scope; for once the menses have ceased, there can be no further birth of a son. Nor should it be suspected of concerning the mother’s property, as that would result in the mother herself being left without any wealth. Therefore, the phrase "when the menses have ceased" refers to the property of the grandfather and others.

<2.3> Furthermore, it is not possible for the cessation of menstruation to be the cause of partition without taking desire into account, because in the absence of desire, there can be no partition. <2.4> When desire exists, upon the inquiry as to whose desire it is, it is determined to be the father's desire alone, based on the statement of Gautama: "After the father's death, the sons shall divide the inheritance; when the mother's menses have ceased and she desires it, while he is still living. [G 28.1–2]

<2.5> Therefore, the non-existence of both parents constitutes a single occasion [for partition]. Because of the use of the dual number in the word "parents" (*pitroḥ*), even when there is a division of the father’s wealth among uterine brothers, the non-existence of the mother alone must be required [as a condition]. <2.6> However, the mention of the mother's non-existence is not for the purpose of a division of the mother’s own wealth; for it would be illogical for the phrase "even while they are living" (*jīvator api*) to refer to the mother’s wealth. Consequently, it must necessarily be stated that this refers to other property. Thus, since the non-existence of both parents is the sole occasion [for partition], and because the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even while they are living" serves to praise the state of their being alive, the non-existence of the mother should not be interpreted as a requirement regarding the mother’s own wealth. This point must be explained in detail.

<2.7> Therefore, there is one time for partition when both parents are deceased, even in the case of ancestral property (paitāmaha-dhana). Likewise, there is another [time]: "when the mother’s menses have ceased, by the father’s will. <2.8> However, there is no partition of that [property] without the father’s will. For it is said: "For they have no power over [the property] while the two [parents] are living" (M 9.104d); likewise: "For they would lack ownership while the father remains free from defect" (D 1563d); likewise: "if he lives and desires [it]" (G 28.2); likewise: "partition of the inheritance with the father’s consent" (Bau 2.2.3.8); likewise: "partition of the inheritance is approved while the father is living" (ŚL 274). Thus, because Manu, Nārada, Gautama, Baudhāyana, Śaṅkha-Likhita, and others have established—without distinction—that while the father is living, the sons’ lack of ownership extends to all ancestral wealth, and that partition is dependent upon the father’s will, and because these authors do not separately state a distinct time for the partition of ancestral wealth, the statements regarding lack of power and the father’s consent must also refer to ancestral wealth.
As for the statement of Yājñavalkya:
"Regarding land acquired by a grandfather, whether as a fixed tenure (*nibandha*) or as physical property, the ownership therein shall be equal for both the father and the son. (YDh 2.121)

This point has been elucidated in truth by the light of the *Naravidyā-vidyā*: where two brothers, whose father is still living and who have not yet received their shares, [one] begets a son and then dies while the other remains alive, and subsequently the father passes away, in that case the son alone obtains that wealth because of extreme proximity (*atisaṃnikarṣa*). To that effect is the statement: "The ownership is equal. Just as the father has ownership over the grandfather's wealth, so too, when he has died, do his sons; in that regard, there is no distinction whatsoever based on proximity or remoteness, because there is no difference in the benefit conferred upon both through the offering of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) according to the *pārvaṇa* rite. This is the intended meaning.

<2.10> For this very reason, even a great-grandson whose father is deceased possesses an equal right [to the estate] together with his son and grandson, because there is no difference in their status as givers of the *piṇḍa* offerings.

<2.11> However, while the father is alive, if the sons possess ownership over the grandfather’s wealth, then upon the division of the property between two brothers—one having sons and one being sonless—the sons of the sonless brother would also receive a share, since there is no difference in their status as owners. <2.12> Nor can it be argued that the statement lacks relevance because it was not introduced [in the context]; for the discussion proceeds specifically concerning those who have multiple fathers.
<2.13> "A fixed obligation" refers to that which has been stipulated: "I shall give this on every Kārttikī. <2.14> "Property" is expressed as a two-word compound because of its association with land.

<2.15> Or rather, this is the meaning of the statement preceded by Dhāreśvara: when a father proceeds to make a division of property out of his own desire, his ownership over the ancestral wealth is equal [to that of his sons]. In that case, he is not entitled to make an unequal division according to his wish, as he might with wealth acquired by himself.

Likewise, Viṣṇu states: "If a father divides his sons, he may, in the case of property acquired by himself, distribute it among them according to his own will; however, in the case of ancestral property, the ownership of father and son is equal" (ViDh 17.1–2). This is very clear: if the father divides the sons, then in the matter of what was acquired by himself, he may give to the sons a distribution that is less or more according to his own desire. But this does not apply to ancestral property, because in that case the ownership is equal; there is no longer freedom of action [for the father].

<2.18> Therefore, both of the following two views must be rejected: [the view] that the statement "the ownership of father and son is equal" is intended to establish equal division of the grandfather’s wealth, or [the view] that it is intended to grant sons independence regarding the division [of the estate]. <2.19> Another statement as well should be explained in exactly this same way.

<2.20> Consequently, it is established that in the case of the grandfather’s wealth and so forth, the father’s share is double, and the division occurs solely by the father’s will, not by the will of the sons.
<2.21> And as for what Manu and Viṣṇu [state]:
But whatever paternal property a father may acquire that was not previously obtained, he need not share that with his sons unless he so desires, as it is self-earned. [M 9.209 = Vi 18.43]

By stating that "one should not divide [the property] against one's will on the grounds that it was self-acquired," these two [authors] demonstrate that even in the case of ancestral wealth (*paitāmaha-dhana*) which was not acquired by oneself, the sons may effect a partition despite the father’s lack of consent; for in that case too, there is an inclination toward the act of giving a partition. Thus, the meaning is that regarding the father’s own acquisitions, he should not divide them against his will, whereas regarding other [wealth], he may divide them even against his will—that is, solely according to his own desire. They do not, however, indicate that a partition occurs merely by the desire of the sons.

<2.22> Furthermore, regarding gems, pearls, and the like, whether inherited from the grandfather or not acquired by the father himself—as if they were self-acquired—the ownership belongs solely to the father, as does the right to bestow unequal shares. As Yājñavalkya states: "The father is the master of all gems, pearls, and corals;
but for all immovable property, neither the father nor the grandfather has such power. [YDh 2.118]

The statement from the *Pitāmaha-śruti* regarding that wealth concerns [movable property]. Because of the inclusion of the phrase "having taken up gems, pearls, and so forth" followed by "of all," the father’s authority over the giving and other transactions of everything *except* land and the like is established; it does not apply to immovable property or pledged assets. Furthermore, because of the inclusion of the word "all" there, the prohibition against giving and so forth applies to whatever is necessary for the maintenance of the family, since the family must necessarily be supported. As Manu says: "The support of those who are to be maintained is praised as a means to attain heaven; in its neglect, however, there is hell. Therefore, one should support them with effort. [M 8.7]
<2.24> However, there is no prohibition against giving and so forth regarding a small amount that does not obstruct one's livelihood, for otherwise the rule would result in meaninglessness.
<2.25> By the inclusion of the term "immovable property," the prohibition against giving and so forth for "encumbrances" and "bipeds" is established by the maxim of the "stick and the cake.

<2.26> Furthermore, if the maintenance of the family cannot even be sustained without the sale of all immovable property and the like, then the sale and so forth of everything is established by implication, according to the statement: "One should protect oneself from everything" (Gītā 9.34).
in the case of immovable property that belongs to the entire lineage and is held in common,
may one person alone effect a sale or a gift without the mutual consent of the others. [Vy 254]
"Whether divided or undivided, sapinda relatives are equal regarding immovable property;
for one individual has no power anywhere in regard to giving, mortgaging, or selling.

[Vyāsa 255] By these two statements of Vyāsa, it must be understood that a single person lacks authority over sale and other such acts. This is because the nature of ownership—defined as the capacity for disposal according to one's will—is no different here than it is with respect to other types of property. However, the statement of Vyāsa is intended to make known that one incurs demerit by obstructing the family through sales, gifts, and so forth, which fall within the domain of a person of evil conduct despite his status as an owner; it does not mean that the sale or other act is legally invalid.
<2.29> And thus,
even if immovable property or bipeds have been acquired by oneself,
there can be neither gift nor sale without having assembled all the sons. [Vy 252]

Such passages as these should be explained in exactly this manner. For instance, the word "must" (*kartavya*) must necessarily be supplied here. Thus, because there is a prohibition against the necessity of giving or selling, a transgression of the injunction occurs by performing those acts; however, there is no non-fulfillment of the act of giving and so forth, since even with a hundred statements one is incapable of making a physical reality otherwise.
For this very reason, Nārada says:
"If many [sons] born of one [father] have separate religious duties and separate activities..."
If they are not agreed upon for the tasks because they possess distinct occupations and qualities,
yet they should give their own shares or even sell them,
they may do all that as they wish, for they are indeed masters of their own property.

<2.32> Let us return to the subject at hand. Thus, because it is untenable to prescribe an equal division between father and son regarding the estate of a grandfather and others according to the aforementioned sequence, and because there is no intention to establish independence for sons in their own partition, this statement is intended either to preclude unequal divisions—whether less or more—that depend upon the will of the progenitor, or to grant equal rights to the son of a deceased brother in relation to his paternal uncle.

<2.33> In this manner, even the division of the grandfather’s wealth should be carried out solely according to the father’s wish; however, the distinction is that [it occurs] "when the menses have ceased. Regarding property acquired by oneself, however, it applies even without the cessation of menses; thus, the rule "after the father's death" is identical in both cases. <2.34> Therefore, there are two periods even regarding the grandfather’s estate.
<2.35> In that regard, when the father himself divides the sons according to his own will, he should take two shares for himself from the grandfather’s wealth and so forth.
"Regarding the division during the father's lifetime, the father himself shall take two shares," so says Bṛhaspati; likewise:
"When dividing [the estate], the father shall receive two shares for himself."
Thus, because it has been established by Nārada without distinction;
furthermore, for this reason as well, the father receives two shares from the grandfather’s wealth:
"The eldest shall have an extra portion of one-twentieth [of the estate] and whatever is the best among all the property."
Half of that shall be for the middle son, and a fourth part for the youngest.
Likewise,
when the preferential share has been thus extracted, one should allot equal shares [to the remainder].
But if their shares have not been extracted, this distribution of portions shall take place:
"The eldest son shall take one share in excess; the next younger than him, one and a half shares; and the youngest sons, one share each"—thus the law is established. (Manu 9.116–117)

By these statements of Manu, the setting aside of one-twentieth, one-half of that, and one-fourth of that—along with the best of all the property—is demonstrated. Likewise, portions consisting of one part plus a half, one part plus a quarter, and one full part are established. Gautama also states: "One-twentieth [of the estate] belongs to the eldest; a pair [of animals], a chariot yoked on both sides, and a breeding bull" (G 28.5). "Pair" refers to goats and the like; "yoked on both sides" refers to horses and the like, as well as a chariot so yoked; and a bull yoked [to a cart]. All this belongs to the eldest. Furthermore: "If there are many animals, those that are one-eyed, lame, humpbacked, or tailless belong to the middlemost" (G 28.6). "Lame" means old; "humpbacked" means of dwarf-like stature; "tailless" means having a deformed tail. These belong to the middlemost if there are many such animals. Likewise: "A sheep, an iron vessel, a house, a yoked cart, and one of each among four-footed animals belong to the youngest; everything else shall be divided equally" (G 28.7–8). Sheep and the rest belong to the youngest; the remainder should all be divided equally. Having thus established this, he states in the sūtra: "Or the first-born may take two shares, and the others one each" (G 28.9–10), whereby two shares for the eldest are prescribed.

<2.38> Nor should it be argued that the eldest son receives two shares by virtue of being the acquirer [of the property], because the rule for two shares is prescribed when the *uddhāra* (preferential share) has not been set aside; furthermore, since the *uddhāra* would be impossible if he were merely the acquirer, and because the middle and youngest sons would be no different from the eldest in their status as acquirers, the prescription of one-and-a-half shares and so forth for them would be untenable, and the terms "eldest" and so forth would be rendered meaningless. <2.39> For this very reason, Manu spoke regarding the division of the father’s wealth between a daughter appointed as an heir (*putrikā*) and a legitimate son (*aurasa*):
"But if, after a daughter has been appointed as an heir, a son is subsequently born..."
"An equal division shall take place there, for there is no seniority for a woman" (M 9.134).
By thus establishing equal shares on the grounds that seniority does not exist due to her being female, this indicates that the man's share consists of two parts.

As it was stated in the *Holākā-adhikaraṇa*, for the sake of establishing the performance of the *holākā* rite by Easterners, a scriptural injunction (*śruti*) stating "the *holākā* should be performed" is postulated; this alone suffices for its establishment. However, a postulation containing words such as "Easterner" and so forth is not accepted due to the complexity of the assumption (*kalpanā-gaurava*). Similarly, in this case as well, one should postulate a scriptural injunction stating that "the purchaser shall take two shares," rather than one containing words such as "father" and so forth.

That is incorrect. In that case, the performance by Easterners is already established by the very general Vedic text (sāmānyaśruti) which must necessarily be inferred; nor can it be argued that a text containing the word "Easterner" (prācya) should be inferred for the purpose of precluding non-Easterners, because their non-performance, being of the nature of a lack of traditional practice (anācāra), cannot serve as the basis for inferring a Vedic text.

In this case, however, because Manu and others employ the term "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*), it is appropriate to postulate a Vedic text containing that very term in order to justify its usage; for there is no necessity to postulate a text containing the term "acquirer" (*arjaka*). Furthermore, when choosing between postulating a text with the term "eldest" or one with the term "acquirer," there is no specific evidence favoring the latter.

Nor should it be argued that, since a Vedic text must necessarily be postulated for the sake of the two shares of the *arjaka* (the acquirer), let that very text be the basis here as well on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*), and let the word "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*) refer to the *arjaka*. For the opposite is also possible; for if one were to postulate a Vedic text containing the word "eldest" specifically for this case, it would be equally possible to postulate that the word "*arjaka*" refers to the "eldest. This is because there is no evidence (*vinigamanā-pramāṇa*) to decide between them. Furthermore, by such means of parsimony and so forth, one might infer some single Vedic text containing three or four words and then claim that all the words of the Smṛti texts have that [Veda] as their ultimate purpose through a figurative or indirect sense (*gauṇī-lakṣaṇā*). In doing so, you have demonstrated your own extreme proficiency in handling the Smṛtis!

Therefore, the meaning of the *Holākā* section is this: since a Vedic text (*śruti*) must necessarily be postulated for any practice or Smṛti statement, and since that very text suffices to justify the portion of the practice and the words of the Smṛti contained therein, no further assumption is required in that regard.

For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha, after stating that the eldest son shall receive two shares, separately prescribed two shares for the one who acquired the property. As it says: "Now follows the division of inheritance among brothers: the eldest shall take two shares" (Va 17.40, 42). Not far from this, he further states: "And whoever among them should have produced [the property], he too shall take two shares" (Va 17.51). If the two shares had already been shown by virtue of being the acquirer, then the mention of two shares for the eldest would be redundant.
<2.42> Even the entitlement to two shares does not arise from seniority alone. As Bṛhaspati says:
"He who is senior by virtue of birth, learning, or qualities shall receive two shares of the inheritance;
the others, however, are entitled to equal shares, but he who is equal to his father shall receive that [share]. [B 26.21]
As regards the status of being an acquirer (*upārjakatva*), [the son] born of two wives—one learned and one of inferior learning—is of no use for the division of the estate.

This twofold division refers specifically to the partition among uterine brothers alone. Furthermore, regarding the partition between uterine and non-uterine brothers, there is the "extra share" (*viṃśoddhāra*) for the eldest. As Bṛhaspati says:
"All sons of twice-born men born of wives of the same caste..."

"Having given the preferential share (*uddhāra*) to the eldest, the others shall divide the remainder equally. [B 26.11] <2.44> Since there is a scriptural injunction for a division preceded by a preferential share among sons born of many wives of equal caste, it is established that the two shares belong exclusively to those who are uterine brothers. And this is logical, because of the greater respect due to them on account of their being uterine brothers. <2.45> Furthermore, the preferential share should not be made out of ten cows and so forth; thus says Manu:
"There is no preferential share (*uddhāra*) for those who have been successful in their own duties among ten [brothers];
rather, something whatsoever should be given to the elder that increases his honor.

(MDh 9.115) Thus, according to the sequence of arguments stated, if the eldest brother alone receives two shares of the father’s wealth, how is it that the father himself—who is capable of giving, selling, or abandoning property, whose connection to the grandfather’s wealth is the very root, and who is most venerable—does not receive two shares of his own father’s wealth?

By the statement, "The eldest is superior by birth, learning, and virtue," Bṛhaspati indicates the instruction that the father receives two shares, by extending to the eldest son the same two shares as the father through the principle of equality with the father. Furthermore, Bṛhaspati has shown this instruction by stating the general rule: "But in the case of partition while the father is alive, let the father himself take two shares" (B 26.16). Likewise, Nārada says:
When dividing his own property, a father may take two shares for himself;
when the husband has died, the mother shall be a sharer with the sons in equal portions.

(N 13.12) <2.47> When the father divides the property, he should take two shares for himself; however, the connection is not "when dividing his own property," because that would contradict what was stated previously.

<2.48> Furthermore, regarding the equal division of ancestral property between father and son, it must be stated that as much wealth as belongs to the father, so much also belongs to the son. It cannot be said that whatever wealth belongs to the father, that same amount alone belongs to the son, for that would result in the two being treated as intermediate [partners] and lead to the undesirable consequence of there being no division between them, as in the case of husband and wife. <2.49> This being the case, when brothers divide their inheritance and the eldest is assigned two shares by virtue of his seniority, if the son of that eldest brother were also assigned two shares, then the eldest brother together with his son would possess four shares while each of the other brothers would have only one share. Moreover, if the eldest brother and his sons were to receive shares equal to those of the father, then the youngest brother would receive only a trifling portion; this would contradict the consensus of the great authorities.

And as for the statement of Bṛhaspati: "In regard to property acquired by the grandfather, whether immovable or movable, equal ownership has indeed been declared for both the father and the son. [B 26.14]

"Equal shares" (*aṃśitvaṃ samam*) means identical. It does not mean that one is entitled to distribute the portions unequally—more or less—according to one's own will, as one might do with property acquired by oneself; rather, its meaning is simply that the share is equal. Alternatively, the statement regarding "equal shares" may refer to the intention of a father who has two fathers (a stepfather). In that case, the statement "there shall be equal ownership" has already been explained previously.

<2.53> Furthermore, if that father is the eldest son who delivers his own father from the hell named Put, then—considering his own brothers—he certainly deserves two shares by virtue of being equal to his father; it is all the more appropriate that he receive two shares in relation to his sons, because the sons' connection to the hereditary wealth is dependent upon the father. On the other hand, if he is not the eldest son of his own father, it is stated that he shall share equally with his own sons.

That is not so; for since even the middle and other sons are ordained to receive one and a half shares and so forth, it is all the more appropriate that the father should have two shares. Furthermore, it is improper both for you and for the sages to state that the father and son have equal shares as a general rule.

<2.55> Furthermore, the claim that the father’s designation of two shares refers only to the property he has himself acquired is also untenable. Since the partition depends upon his will, and since by virtue of that will even two, three, fewer, or more shares could be obtained, the injunction would be rendered purposeless. Nor should the statement be described as having a restrictive purpose (*niyamārthatva*), because that would contradict Viṣṇu. As he says: "If the father divides the sons, his own will prevails regarding property acquired by himself; however, in the case of ancestral property, the ownership of father and son is equal" (ViDh 17.12). <2.56> The meaning of this is: regarding what he has acquired himself, whatever he desires to take—whether half, two shares, or three—all of that is permitted by the scripture for him; but this does not apply even to ancestral property.

Likewise, Hārīta states: "Or, while still living, he may divide [the estate] and retire to the forest, or enter the stage of the aged (*vṛddhāśrama*); or, having divided it with a small portion, he may live taking the greater part for himself. If it should appear that [the property] has diminished, he may take more from them. By this, the division of a small portion and the taking of the majority of the wealth by the father are prescribed; the "stage of the aged" refers to renunciation (*pravrajyā*).

And as for the statement of Śaṅkha and Likhita: "If he should have only one son, he should make two shares for himself" [ŚL 268], its meaning is this: *ekaputraḥ* means "one who has one son. It is not, however, a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "he for whom there is only one son," because a *bahuvrīhi*, being predominant in its external referent (*anyapadārthapradhānatvena*), is weaker than a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*.

The legitimate son (*aurasa*) is the only one son; such a father is entitled to two shares. However, the statement that "even though the *kṣetraja* is the son of the father, his ownership therein is not equal" must be understood as referring specifically to the father of the *kṣetraja*. For the *kṣetraja* has two fathers. Thus Baudhāyana says: "He who is begotten on the wife of one who is deceased, impotent, or diseased, with the consent of another, is known as the *kṣetraja*. (BaudhDhS 2.2.3.17)

"He indeed has two fathers and belongs to two gotras; he becomes the recipient of the *svadhā* offering and a sharer of the inheritance from both. (Baudhāyana Dharma Sūtra 2.2.3.18). The meaning of this is: one born in the wife of a eunuch or similar person, with her consent and by another man, is a *kṣetraja* son. Thus says Nārada: "When seed is sown in the field with the consent of the owner of the field..."

"The offspring of those two is considered to belong to both the seed-owner and the owner of the field" (N 12.58). Consequently, regarding the injunction that "one who has only one son shall divide his property into two shares," the fact that having only one son is intended as a qualification of the agent (the subject) makes it appropriate to regard it as significant; thus, the claim that it is not intended because it is a qualification of the thing to be enjoined (the object) is also refuted. Furthermore, by declaring at every moment that the words employed by Manu, Gautama, Dakṣa, and others—who are supremely discerning—lack any intended meaning, you are directly proclaiming your own lack of intentionality.

<2.65> Likewise, even regarding wealth acquired by a son, the father is entitled to two shares; for there is an undifferentiated scriptural statement: "two shares" and "they shall take two shares. Kātyāyana has stated this very clearly:
"By virtue of having acquired the wealth, the father takes two shares or half;
and when the father has died, the mother also receives a share equal to that of a son. [K 851]
The meaning of this is that, due to the son's acquisition of wealth, the father shall receive either two shares or one half-share.

Nor should it be said that "son" (*putra*) and "wealth" (*vitta*) constitute "son-and-wealth" (*putravitta*), and that because of the acquisition of these two, the father is entitled to two shares, whereas because of the non-acquisition by the sons, he takes everything. For even in the case of one who has not acquired [wealth] himself, when there is a division with his brothers, it is accepted that he receives two shares by virtue of being the acquirer of wealth; how then could he take everything? Therefore, it must be stated that while the acquirer receives two shares when a relative entitled to a share exists, he takes everything only when such a person does not exist. If this were so, the terms "father" and "son" would be the utterances of someone speaking in error. Furthermore, "acquisition" (*arjana*) is an activity that serves as the cause for ownership (*svatva*); to say that "acquisition does not produce ownership" is a contradiction. Moreover, it was demonstrated in the section on the gift of all one's property (*sarvasvadāna*) that there is no ownership over one's sons. Consequently, in that context, the term "acquirer" is used figuratively regarding the son, while it is used in its primary sense regarding wealth; and this cannot be possible for a single word heard only once.

<2.68> It should not be argued that this rule is redundant because, since the wealth was acquired by the son, he would naturally receive two shares, and since the father would also receive two shares even without this statement (due to general principles), the result would be equal division. This is because, even in the absence of this specific statement, the father’s claim to two shares over the son’s own acquired wealth does not arise; thus, the statement serves a purpose. <2.69> Furthermore, if the phrase "from the acquisition of wealth by the son" were restricted to the father's estate, then the options of receiving two shares or half a share based on the father's wish would be untenable. Since the taking of the portion depends on the father's will, and because such a will is unpredictable, it is possible for him to take one and a half, three-quarters, or one-quarter of a share; how then could there be a mention of only these two alternatives? Moreover, it has already been stated previously that a restrictive rule regarding the father's estate is not possible here. In this context, it is logical that just as the son receives two shares of the wealth he himself acquired, he likewise receives half of that same wealth [if it is part of the paternal estate].

<2.70> Furthermore, the statement is not intended for the purpose of grasping one share as being half of two shares. This is because, since both "half" and "two shares" are parts of a whole, there is a mutual requirement for a single part. Moreover, since the two are equal in their status as qualifiers of the person and as objects of the act of taking, a reciprocal relationship between them is untenable. Since there is no dispute that the ablative ending in *vittārjanāt* ("from the acquisition of wealth") is used to provide a referent for the connection with the part consisting of "two shares," it is likewise proper that it connects with the word "half. Furthermore, because there is no intervention between the words *vittārjana* and *ardha*, it is understood to be half of the wealth itself; it is not understood as one share being half of two shares. And since the term *ekāṃśa* ("one share") could have been employed at will, it is improper to use a non-expressive term; therefore, it is logical that it refers to half of the wealth itself.

<2.71> In that regard, if there is depletion of the paternal estate, half of the wealth acquired by the son belongs to the father, while the son who acquired it receives two shares and the others receive one share each. However, if there is no depletion, the father receives two shares, the acquirer likewise receives exactly that much, and the others have no share at all. <2.72> Alternatively, a father endowed with qualities such as learning may take half [of the estate], since we see that the eldest alone receives an additional share on account of learning and the like; whereas a father devoid of learning and such qualities receives two shares merely by virtue of being the progenitor.

<2.73> From wealth inherited in succession or from wealth acquired by a son, the father himself shall take two shares. The meaning of the statement is that he is not entitled to more than this, even if he should desire it. However, from wealth acquired by himself, he may take as much as he wishes to take.

<2.74> Regarding sons, however, a father may divide the paternal estate after giving a twentieth part as a preferential share (*uddhāra*) to some, or even without giving one; or, from wealth acquired by himself, he may—acting righteously—make an unequal division out of a desire to give more, whether for the sake of honoring those possessed of superior qualities, for the sake of maintaining a large family, out of compassion for those who are incapable, or out of affection for those who are devoted. <2.75> Thus says Yājñavalkya: "An unequal division made by a father is declared to be lawful" (YDh 2.116cd). Likewise, Bṛhaspati:
"Those shares which have been assigned by the father as equal, deficient, or excessive must be maintained exactly as they were; otherwise, they should be subject to correction. Thus says Nārada.

But for those who have been divided by the father with unequal shares of wealth—some more, some less—that very division shall be lawful, for the father is the master of all. (N 13.15) <2.76> Because he is the cause of ownership over all the wealth, and because such ownership is impossible in the case of ancestral property (*paitāmaha*), this lawful division into unequal shares made by the father applies only to the father’s own wealth. And thus Viṣṇu says: “If the father divides his sons, he has full freedom regarding property acquired by himself; but in ancestral property, the ownership of father and son is equal. (Vi 17.12)

<2.77> Now, if the father should effect a partition, he may divide his sons according to his own will; either by giving the eldest a superior share, or all may be equal sharers. [Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.114]
Since the Yājñavalkya statement indicates that the "extra portion" (*uddhāra*) constitutes the superior share, how can it be asserted that [the other shares] may be less or more than that?

It is said in reply: Since the superior share consisting of the *viṃśoddhāra* (the twentieth part) is already established when a division is made by the brothers even after the father has passed away, the statement would be purposeless if its aim were that [share]. <2.78> Now, if it is argued that the statement is intended to ensure the legality of the equal shares (*samāṃśatā*) established by the father even in the absence of such a preferential share (*uddhāra*), that is not so; for in that case, only a reduction [of the share] made by the father would be legal, and thus the word "additional" (*adhika*) would be redundant. <2.79> Furthermore, if the description of "deficiency" and "excess" were intended to refer to the preferential share, then the phrase "he may divide according to his wish" (*icchayā vibhajet*) would be purposeless, because what is to be expressed is already stated by the other three words.

In this view, however, the rule "one may divide according to one's wish" refers to wealth acquired by oneself; whereas the rules regarding the superior share (*śreṣṭhāṃśa*) and equal shares refer to ancestral wealth (*paitāmaha-dhana*). Thus, nothing is redundant. Furthermore, even when the father has passed away, Bṛhaspati has described two types of partition: "The partition for heirs is shown to be of two kinds: one according to the order of seniority of age, and the other an arrangement of equal shares. (B 26.17)

He demonstrates the preferential share according to the order of seniority: "Likewise, equality of shares is the other way. Since the mutual division among brothers is of two kinds, there would be no distinction made by the father. Thus says Nārada: "Or the father himself, being advanced in age, may divide his sons; he may give the eldest a superior share, or as his mind may determine. (N 13.4)

<2.82> Having stated the superior share for the eldest, the phrase "again, as his mind might incline" indicates that this distribution—whether deficient or excessive—is distinct from the superior share; for it is understood as a separate distribution in which the father’s intention must be exercised due to the previously mentioned reasons. <2.83> Furthermore, regarding the statement of Nārada:
"One who is diseased, one who is angry, and one whose mind is attached to sensual objects..."

And "the father is not the master in partitioning if he acts contrary to the scriptures" (N 13.16); this refers to a case where, due to a distracted mind caused by illness and so forth, or out of anger toward a certain son, or out of affection for the son of a favorite wife, he partitions [the estate] contrary to the scriptures. However, because of the previously mentioned reasons, an unequal partition that is in accordance with the scriptures is indeed valid. As Kātyāyana says:
Upon the division of property while the father is still living, he shall not treat one son as distinct from the others;
nor shall he disinherit one suddenly, without cause.

<2.85> One should not distinguish [one son] from another by giving him an excessive share, nor should one exclude him—that is, one should not deprive him of his share—without a valid reason. For distinctions such as the *uddhāra* (preferential portion) apply only to many sons, not to a single one. Even for a single son, no distinction should be made without a reason; however, it must indeed be done on account of a reason. Because of the understanding that "even for a single one," this distinction does not depend on the *uddhāra*, but rather is produced solely by the father's will; thus, the meaning is exactly as stated.
<2.86> Furthermore, if the sons themselves seek a partition while the father is still living, then an unequal division must not be granted by the father. Regarding this, Manu says:
"If there should be a joint effort among brothers who have not yet divided their inheritance, the father must under no circumstances grant them an unequal share. (M 9.215)

<2.87> However, in that case, the father must indeed grant him a share (*uddhāra*), because there is no absence of the nature of an unequal division; for it is only the prohibition of an unequal distribution—whether deficient or excessive—that is intended.
<2.88> Thus concludes the partition made by the father.
CHAPTER 3.
<3.1> Now, the partition among brothers when the father has passed away is discussed.

Furthermore, it is stated that even though the sons acquire ownership of the wealth upon the death of the father, a lawful partition among uterine brothers does not take place while the mother is still living; this is because the phrase "after both the father and the mother" indicates that the division of the paternal estate occurs only upon the death of both parents.

<3.2> Furthermore, [the phrase] "after the mother" (*mātuḥ ūrdhvam*) cannot mean for the purpose of dividing the mother’s wealth, because from the term *paitṛkam* (paternal) one understands the division of the father’s wealth alone, and there is no evidence for assuming that the word *paitṛkam* is a *ekaśeṣa* compound [meaning both paternal and maternal]. <3.3> Moreover, since the division of her wealth would already be stated by the very words "when the mother has passed away" (*jananyāṃ saṃsthitāyām*), the phrase "after the mother" would be redundant.
<3.4> Likewise, Yājñavalkya says:
"After the death of both parents, the sons shall divide the inheritance and the debt equally."

"The daughters [inherit] the remainder of the mother's [estate]; in their absence, the lineage [inherits]. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.117) The fact that daughters have no right to the division of the mother’s property when they exist, but that sons have the right by means of the term "lineage" (anvaya) when they do not exist, is established by the latter half of this verse alone. As for the phrase "of the parents" (pitrōḥ) in the first half, it refers exclusively to the father’s property; otherwise, there would be the fault of tautology. By stating that "brothers shall divide [the estate] upon the death of both the mother and the father," the author prescribes the interval between the deaths of both as the occasion for partition; thus, their conjunction (sāhitya) is intended.

And likewise, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "For the family has its root in the inheritance. Those who have a father are not independent; the same applies to those whose mother is still living. They declare that even in relation to their mother, they are not independent and are not entitled to a partition.
Vyāsa has stated this very clearly:
"While both parents are alive, co-residence among brothers is prescribed."

In the absence of that [father], the dharma of those who have divided [the inheritance] increases. [Vy 247] <3.9> Since the prohibition against partition is established by way of prescribing co-residence, and since partition is prohibited while the father and mother are living—by the phrase "while they both live" (*jīvatoḥ*)—the conjunction is not intended to be significant. Therefore, even if only one [of the two parents] is living, partition is not lawful; rather, it is lawful only when both are deceased. <3.10> Thus says Bṛhaspati:
The partition among brothers has been demonstrated for the case of the absence of both parents;
it is also commended when the mother’s menses have ceased, even while they both are living.

[B 26.9] Since, while the mother is living and her menses have ceased, a partition cannot logically concern the mother's share, and since the commendation of the partition "even while they both are living"—which is indicated by the word "also" (*api*)—refers specifically to that partition mentioned in the case of the absence of both, it is determined that the partition among brothers in the absence of both refers exclusively to the father's estate.

<3.12> For this very reason, Vyāsa prescribes a partition in which the deceased is the primary consideration while the mother is still living: "When sons of the same caste and number are born to one man from different mothers, the share of the mother is recommended for them. [Vy 249]

Likewise, Bṛhaspati says: "If many sons born of one [father] are equal in number according to their respective mothers' castes, they should divide the inheritance according to the shares of their mothers, in accordance with dharma. [B 26.24]

<3.13> Since there is no distinction in the division of sons based on equality of caste or number, this division belongs to the mother alone and not to the sons; thus, the division must be made with reference to her. Consequently, as in the case of the property of other mothers, even here, while the mother is living, the sons have no independence regarding a mutual division among themselves. Rather, a division is only lawful (dharmya) by the mother’s consent alone. <3.14> Therefore, that which was stated by Gautama and others—"But upon division, there is an increase in dharma" [G 28.4], etc.—is to be understood as referring to the time after the mother's death.

<3.15> In that case, if they wish to remain undivided, then the eldest alone, being capable of providing for their welfare (*yogakṣema*), shall take the whole; the others should depend upon him just as they did on their father. As Manu says: "The eldest alone shall take the paternal wealth in its entirety;
the rest should depend upon him just as they did on their father" (M 9.105).

Likewise, Gautama states: "Or the entire estate belongs to the eldest; he shall support the others like a father. By the use of the word "or," they may either live separately or live together. And living together occurs only by the will of all, as Nārada says: "The eldest brother, if capable, shall support all his brothers like a father, or a younger brother who is capable; for in the family, the matter depends upon capability."
Even the youngest son, if capable, shall maintain all [the others]; here, the middle son’s duty is established by the logic of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpanyāya*).
It was stated previously that partition may occur even for a single person by his own will. For this very reason, Kātyāyana, having introduced the subject of partition, says:
"The wealth of those who have not attained legal capacity shall be kept free from expenditure."

And likewise, they should entrust [the property] to kinsmen and friends of those who have gone abroad. Furthermore, there is the statement: "The wealth of a minor shall be protected until he reaches legal majority" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.48).

This division among sons is uniform, extending through sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons. In this matter, the order of entitlement is not determined by the sequence of proximity based on biological descent; for it is only for the three—sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons—that the offering of the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha is prescribed, as it involves the offering of two rice-balls (*piṇḍas*): one for the deceased father and two for his ancestors. For this very reason, Devala says:
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather,
wait upon the newborn son like birds at a peepal tree;
[they do so] with honey, meat, vegetables, milk, and milk-rice.
"He will offer us the *śrāddha* during the rainy season under the asterism Maghā.
Likewise, Śaṅkha, Likhita, and Yama state:
"The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather."
They praise a son who has been born, just as birds praise the *pippala* tree:
"With honey, meat, rhinoceros flesh, milk, or milk-rice,
he will grant us satisfaction during the rainy season under the asterism of Maghā."
Because of the mention of the *prapitāmaha* (great-grandfather), the term "son" (*putra*) extends in scope up to the *prapautra* (great-grandson).

Therefore, since the performance of the *śrāddha* offering by one as far as the great-grandson results in benefit for those as far as the great-grandfather, the right to inherit (*dāyādhikāra*) is equal for all members down to the great-grandson. <3.19> For this very reason, in the case of two [sons] whose fathers are living—namely, the grandson and the great-grandson—their entitlement is restricted because they lack the eligibility for the *pārvaṇa* rite and thus do not offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*).
<3.20> Upon the death of both parents, however, the specific distinction made by the father ceases for the brothers; everything else, however, must be understood to remain exactly the same.

<3.21> And when there is one son on one side and several sons on the other side, then the one son receives one share and the other belongs to the many grandsons; for since the connection to the wealth is rooted in the birth of their respective fathers, they too have a right to exactly as much wealth as he has a right to as its owner. <3.22> And as it is said: "In the case of those who have multiple fathers, the allotment of shares is according to the fathers" (Yājñavalkya 2.120cd = Viṣṇu 27.23ab).

This statement does not apply to that case. Since all that wealth belongs specifically to the paternal uncle’s father, it would belong entirely to the paternal uncle alone, and not to his brothers' sons. If the allotment of shares were made according to the father—as in the case of a division between a father and his sons—the paternal uncle would receive two shares due to his connection with two fathers' portions, whereas each of the brothers' sons would receive only one share; in that event, there would be a contradiction with established custom (*śiṣṭācāra*). However, this [rule] applies to a case where one brother has few sons and the other has many; in such a situation, the allotment of shares is indeed according to the father.
<3.24> Now follows the partition among sons of the same caste. There is an option: either preceded by a twentieth-share (*viṃśoddhāra*) and so forth, or an equal division alone.

<3.25> Hārīta states that even without a preferential share, there may be an equal division, following the word "when the father" (*pitari*): "When [the father] has died, the division of the inheritance is equal. Likewise Uśanas:
"This division has been proclaimed for those of the castes born in the direct order (*ānulomya*)."
"For those of the same caste, an equal division is prescribed.
And so says Paiṭhīnasi: "When paternal inheritance is being divided, the division shall be equal. Likewise Yājñavalkya:
"After the death of both parents, the sons shall divide the estate and the debt equally."
Therefore, there is an option between division with and without the *uddhāra* (preferential share).

<3.26> Nor should it be argued that because even a purely equal division is sanctioned by scripture, it alone must be performed as a mandatory rule; for since an *uddhāra* may also be permitted among brothers out of an excess of devotion, there is an option, just as there is between division and non-division. <3.27> For this very reason, in the world today, only an equal division is observed, due to the absence of an excess of devotion and the lack of an eldest brother entitled to an *uddhāra*.

<3.28> However, he who, out of consideration for his own fitness alone, is indifferent to the partition of the wealth of his father, grandfather, and so forth, should be given even a small amount—such as a handful of rice—and then divided [from the rest] in order to eliminate future distress for him and his family. Regarding this, Manu says: "But among brothers, he who, though capable by his own labor, does not desire the wealth, shall be excluded from his share after being given something for his subsistence. [M 9.207]
Likewise, Yājñavalkya states:
"For one who is capable but makes no effort, partition may be made after giving him something.

(YDh 2.116ab) Furthermore, when the father has passed away and partition is being made by the uterine brothers, a share equal to that of a son must be given to the mother, because of the scriptural statement: "The mother is an inheritor of an equal share" (NSm 13.12c).

<3.30> Since the term *mātṛpada* refers to one's own mother, it does not refer to the mother of a co-wife; for it is impossible for a single word heard once to have both a primary and a secondary meaning. <3.31> Furthermore, when the woman’s property (*strīdhana*) is being divided, the mother receives an equal share with the brothers and others; however, if it has already been given, she receives half. And when the father distributes an equal division among his sons, he must grant all the wives an equal share corresponding to their sons. Thus says Yājñavalkya:
If he should divide the shares equally, the wives must be made equal sharers,

provided that no separate property (strīdhana) has been given to them by the husband or by the father-in-law. To a wife who has been superseded by another wife, an equal amount as compensation for the supersession (ādhivedanika) must be given.
To those women for whom no woman’s property (*strīdhana*) has been given, one should assign half [of the share].
(Yājñavalkya 2.148) <3.32> And wives who are childless shall receive equal shares, not those who have sons. Thus Vyāsa says:
"The wives of a father who has no sons are declared to be entitled to equal shares."
And all those paternal grandmothers are proclaimed to be equal to mothers.

Likewise, Viṣṇu states: "Mothers are entitled to shares according to the shares of their sons; so too are unmarried daughters. (Vi 18.34–35) <3.33> "According to the shares of their sons" means that just as the sons receive four, three, two, or one share respectively according to the order of the castes, so it is for the wives as well. <3.34> For unmarried daughters, following the share of the son, it is one-fourth of that. Thus says Bṛhaspati:
"The mothers shall have equal shares, but the maiden daughters shall have one-fourth of a share. (B 26.22cd)
<3.35> Three shares for the son and one share for the daughter. As Kātyāyana says:
"For unmarried daughters, a fourth share is prescribed;
for sons, three shares are ordained as their ownership in the case of small property. [K 858]

<3.36> From their own shares, the sons of those with little wealth should draw out a fourth part and give it to the daughters. Thus says Manu: "The brothers shall severally give to the sisters from their own shares a fourth part of each respective portion; those who are unwilling to give would become outcasts. [M 9.118]

Because of the scriptural injunction that "they should give" (*pradadyuḥ*) and because of the scriptural statement regarding the state of being an outcast (*patitatva*) for one who does not give, daughters must not be accepted with the notion that they possess a right [to inheritance]. For one brother does not give from his own share to another brother who lacks such a right.
As Yājñavalkya says:
"But those who have not been consecrated should be consecrated by their brothers who have already been consecrated."
"And having given a fourth part from her own share to the sisters" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.124).

This [text] states that sisters are to be consecrated [with sacraments], not that they have a right of inheritance. And thus, when there is abundant wealth, it is established that the wealth appropriate for marriage must be given, and there is no rule restricting it to a fourth part.

Furthermore, this should be understood to apply when the number of daughters and sons is equal. When the numbers are unequal, either the greater portion of the wealth would go to the daughter alone, or the son would be left without a share; and this is not proper, because of the son's preeminence.
<3.41> And as for this objection stated here:

"Even when the father's property does not exist, the sacramental rites must necessarily be performed by the brothers who have already been consecrated, having extracted [the funds] from their own shares. [N 13.34]

"Based on these words of Nārada, and because the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) of a sister must necessarily be performed, even her exclusion from inheritance (*niraṃśatā*) is not a fault. This is incorrect, because this statement is intended for the purpose of performing the sacramental rites for brothers. Furthermore, the reading "by the brothers who have already been consecrated" (*bhrātṛṇāṃ pūrvasaṃskṛtaiḥ*) lacks an authoritative source, and the context here is the sacramental rite of brothers. For this was stated previously:
"But for those whose ritual procedures of consecration were not performed by the father in due order... [3.42]
The funeral rites for those [deceased brothers] must be performed by their [surviving] brothers from that very paternal wealth.

Because of the masculine designation in the words "for those" (*yeṣāṃ teṣām*) and because the statement "immediately after them" (*tadanantaram eva*) begins with the condition of their being absent, this rule is intended solely for the purpose of performing the *saṃskāra* (funeral rites) for the brothers.
Thus ends the section on the division of the property of the father, grandfather, and others.
CHAPTER FOUR,
SECTION ONE <4.1.1> Now, for the purpose of dividing the woman’s property, the woman’s property is first defined.

Regarding this, Viṣṇu states: "That which is given by the father, mother, son, or brother; that which is received at the nuptial fire; that given on account of supersession; that given by a kinsman; the dowry (*śulka*); and the subsequent gift (*anvādheya*)—these constitute the woman’s property.
(ViDh 17.18) Kātyāyana explains the *anvādheya*:
"Whatever is obtained by a woman from her husband's family after the marriage..."
That which is declared to be *anvādheya* (a woman’s separate property) is what she receives from her husband’s family; likewise,
whatever she obtains after the marriage rite,
whether out of affection from her husband or from her parents, that is *anvādheya*, according to Bhṛgu.

<4.1.3> By the term *bandhu* (kinsman), the mother and father are included. Thus, the meaning is this: that wealth which is obtained after marriage from kinsmen through the medium of the mother and father, as well as from the husband and the husband’s family, such as the father-in-law and so forth—that wealth is *anvādheya*. Furthermore, in the statement of Viṣṇu, the word *bandhu* refers to maternal uncles and others, because the father and other paternal relatives have already been specified by their own names; for regarding what is obtained at the time of marriage, the right of ownership belongs either to the husband or to the parents, depending on whether the form of marriage is *brāhma*, *āsura*, or otherwise.

<4.1.4> Manu and Kātyāyana state what constitutes a woman’s property: "That which is received before the nuptial fire, that which is brought by the husband, that which is given out of affection, and that which is received from her brother, mother, or father—this is declared to be the sixfold property of a woman. [M 9.194 = K 894]
