"Regarding that which was taken away by the grandfather and subsequently acquired by the father through his own power—whether obtained by means of learning, valor, or other such means—the ownership therein is traditionally held to belong to the father. [B 26.58]
One may make a gift at one's own will, and likewise enjoy [the wealth] from that property;
in the absence of such [a person], the sons are declared to have equal shares.
[B 26.59] By the phrase "according to one's own capacity," he indicates the exertion of the body and the use of non-common property.

<6.2.36> In both statements, the word "father" (*pitṛ*) is used figuratively (*upalakṣaṇa*), because the reason given is "that which was acquired by oneself. <6.2.37> Thus, one should understand that the same legal arrangement applies to property other than land—even when inherited through succession—in cases where it is of such a nature as being self-acquired. <6.2.38> But regarding land, Śaṅkha states an exception: "If a man alone recovers land that was previously lost through his own effort, others shall share it according to their respective portions after he has given them a fourth part. [ŚL 273]

<6.2.39> Although the particle *eva* indicates that the labor involves exclusively uncommon wealth and physical exertion, nevertheless, for the rescuer, it is not uncommon [to receive a reward]. Rather, a fourth part plus an additional share of the reclaimed land should be given to him. This is because of the force of the word "land" (*bhūmi*) and because there is no reason to disregard that meaning.
<6.2.40> Thus concludes the determination of what is divisible and what is indivisible.

<7.2.1> Now, the partition of property acquired after partition is described. Regarding this, Manu and Nārada state:

Thus said Bṛhan-Manu: "The sons of the Brāhmaṇī wife shall take the land acquired as a religious gift (brahmadāya)."

All twice-born (dvija) castes have a right to the house, as well as to land inherited by succession (kramāgata). Since the term "inherited by succession" is used without qualification, it refers to land received through the lineage from one's grandfather, great-grandfather, and so forth, establishing a connection with all twice-born castes. Furthermore, regarding land acquired through gift (pratigraha), the prohibition of eligibility applies specifically to the sons of Kṣatriyas and others, which implies that even grandsons and subsequent descendants are not authorized. Bṛhaspati says:
"Land received as a gift must certainly not be given to the son of a Kṣatriya or other such caste."

"Even if his father should give it, when he is dead, the son of a Brahmin shall take it. (B 26.121) And thus, it is stated that land received as a gift is indeed "obtained through the inheritance of Brahman"; for "Brahman" refers to the Veda, since the rule for receiving such land is based on one's possession of its study and knowledge of its meaning. It is not, however, land obtained through the worship mentioned by Manu, as in:
"He should be a worshiper of those Brahmins who have returned from the teacher’s house. (MDh 3.108)
"For this imperishable Brāhma ordinance is prescribed for kings," because it consists of the nature of worship.
Alternatively, one [type of gift] is prohibited by one [text], and the other by another.

<9.22> However, land is not a *brahmadāya* (a gift to a Brāhmaṇa). This is because the connection of the twice-born with land inherited through succession is established by scriptural injunction, and because it is specifically forbidden for a Śūdra alone. As Bṛhaspati states: "One born of a Śūdra woman by twice-born men does not deserve a share of land; he shall receive everything from his own caste—thus the law is settled. [B 26.122]

<9.23> Since only land is specified as the object of acquisition, it is established that even when land has been obtained by a twice-born man through purchase, a gift, or other means, a Śūdra has no right to it.

<9.24> However, if a Brāhmaṇa has an only son who is a Śūdra, he is entitled to one-third share; two shares go to the *sapiṇḍas*. Either a *sapiṇḍa* or a *sakulya* shall give the *svadhā* offerings or take the inheritance.

If there is only a single Śūdra son for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, he shall take half of that wealth; the other half they shall take according to the order of succession to the property of a sonless man to be described later. And it should be understood that this entitlement to a third part and the right to take half belong to one who is endowed with learning, discipline, and virtue. As Manu says:
"Whether there be a legitimate son or even if there be no son at all, one should not, according to the law, give more than a tenth part to the son of a Śūdra woman. (M 9.154)

By this [verse], since the prohibition against giving more than a tenth part of the estate applies even when there is no son of a twice-born caste, it is understood that the preceding [rule] refers specifically to the case of a son born of an excellent Śūdra woman. And as for that which was stated by Manu:
"The son of a Śūdra woman from Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas does not inherit the estate;
whatever his father may give to him, that alone shall be his wealth" (M 9.155).

By this, his entitlement to inherit the estate is indeed prohibited; however, it should be understood that this applies provided he receives a tenth part of the wealth obtained through his father’s favor.
Bṛhaspati states this as well:
"A virtuous son born of a Śūdra womb who serves a childless [father]..."

The sapinda relatives shall obtain the remainder for their livelihood; this means that something should be given for the purpose of subsistence through agriculture and other such means. For one who lacks merit, the means of subsistence—food and so forth—should be provided through the rule governing a pupil (*antevāsī*) by way of quartering service (*pāda-śuśrūṣā*). And as Manu says:
"If a Brāhmaṇa, out of lust, should beget a son upon a Śūdra woman..."

"Because he completes his strength (*śavas*) at that very point, he is therefore known as a *pāraśava*. (M 9.178) This refers to the son of an unmarried Śūdra woman, because approaching a married wife only once during her season is prescribed by law, and conception occurs only then, not even upon subsequent unions. As Yājñavalkya states:
"When a brother dies without a son, one may approach that [widow] only once during her season. (Y?)
Likewise, Manu says:

"Having approached her according to the rule—she being dressed in white garments and pure in her observances—he should unite with her in private once during each fertile period, until she has given birth. (MDh 9.70)
If the mere first approach were the cause of conception, the singular mention [of the act] would serve a visible purpose; otherwise, its purpose would have to be assumed as invisible (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

For this very reason, even in common worldly practice, the counting of months is observed starting from the day of the first contact, for the sake of auspicious customs and for rites such as the *puṃsavana* and *sīmantonnayana*, which are prescribed for specific months.
Therefore, the injunction "one may procreate a son out of desire" refers exclusively to an unmarried Śūdra woman.
Furthermore, the son of a Śūdra born of an unmarried slave-woman or similar Śūdra woman, with the father’s permission, shall receive a share equal to that of the other sons. As Manu says:
"Whether born of a slave-woman or the slave-woman of a slave, whatever son may be born to a Śūdra, he shall, being permitted, take a share; such is the established law" (M 9.179).
But without her consent, he is entitled to only half a share. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"Even one born of a Śūdra woman by a Śūdra through desire shall be a sharer of a portion;
when the father has died, the brothers should make him a recipient of half a share. (YDh 2.133cd–134ab)

However, if there is no daughter’s son (*dauhitra*), one whose wife has been married off and who has no brothers shall take the entire estate. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says: "One who has no brothers shall take everything, except for the sons of the daughters" (YDh 2.134cd). If a daughter’s son exists, they should divide the property equally and take it, because no specific distinction is heard in the texts. For, even though he was born to an unmarried woman, he possesses the status of a son; whereas the other, although belonging to the lineage of a married woman, possesses the status of a daughter’s son. Therefore, it is logical that they receive equal shares.

This is because she does not perform the duties of an eldest son by her own nature, but rather becomes the giver of the funeral oblations (*piṇḍa*) through the medium of her own son. Thus Manu says:

"I shall give you an unbrothered maiden, adorned;
whatever son is born of her shall be my son. [VaDh 17.17]

[The text] states that only the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) possesses the status of a son; by that, it implies the status of "son" belongs to both the appointed daughter and her son. That is not so, because it contradicts Manu. His status as a son is merely figurative (*gauṇa*), based solely on his connection to the offering of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*). It is precisely through him that the appointed daughter becomes an offerer of the cake, since one [the son] does so inherently while the other [the mother] does so by virtue of that connection. Furthermore, when the appointed daughter and the legitimate son (*aurasa*) are of the same caste (*savarṇa*), the aforementioned division of inheritance should be understood to apply. However, if they are of different castes, the division must be made exactly as in the case of a legitimate son of a different caste, because the appointed daughter and the legitimate son are equal in this respect.

Furthermore, if a daughter who has been formally appointed (*putrikā*) dies as a widow or is determined to be barren without having produced a son, she has no right to her father’s property; for she was appointed as a *putrikā* for the sake of performing ancestral rites (*svadhākara*) through a son, and in his absence, she is equivalent to any other daughter.

<10.7> Regarding the division among the *aurasa* (legitimate) son, the *kṣetraja* (son born of the wife), and the others: those sons who are of the same caste as the father but of a higher caste than the *aurasa* son—namely the *putrikāputra* (son of an appointed daughter), *kṣetraja*, *kānīna* (maiden-born), *gūḍhaja* (secretly born), *apaviddha* (cast off), *sahoḍha* (born with the bride), *paunarbhava* (son of a remarried woman), *dattaka* (given son), *svayamupāgata* (self-offered), *kṛtaka* (adopted), and *krīta* (bought)—are entitled to one-third of the share of the *aurasa* son. To this effect, Devala, after enumerating the twelve types of sons, states: "These twelve sons have been declared for the sake of continuity, including those born of oneself, those born of another, and those obtained by chance. [D 1582]
Of these, the first six are kinsmen and heirs; the other six belong to the father alone.
Furthermore, among the sons, the distinction is determined by their successive order.
For all these are declared to be heirs to the property of one who has no son of the body (aurasa).
When they are born again from a different womb, seniority among them no longer exists.
Among them, those sons who are of the same caste as their father shall receive a third share;
those of lower caste shall live under him, provided with food and clothing.

<10.8> The six [sons], beginning with the legitimate son (*aurasa*), are not only heirs to the father’s estate, but are also heirs to the property of their paternal kinsmen, such as the *sapiṇḍas* and others. Others, being of a different lineage, are heirs to the father’s estate alone, and not to that of the *sapiṇḍas* and others. <10.9> In the case of a father who has no legitimate son, they take the entire inheritance; however, when a legitimate son exists, they receive a one-third share. <10.10> Since the appointed daughter (*putrikā*) is equal to a legitimate son, this same order of distribution applies to her as well.

<10.11> However, those sons of lower caste than the father who are of higher caste than the legitimate son (aurasa) shall receive a fifth or sixth share of the legitimate son’s portion, depending on their qualities and merits. As Manu says: "But when dividing the paternal inheritance, the legitimate son should give a sixth part of the father's wealth to the son born of the wife, or even a fifth. [M 9.164]

<10.12> Since the statement of Devala declares that all [sons] are equal to the *kṣetraja* son, the term "*kṣetraja*" in the statement of Manu is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). <10.13> However, those who are of lower caste than their father or their uterine brother have no right beyond mere food and clothing. Regarding this, Manu says:
"The *aurasa* son alone is the master of the paternal wealth."
"But for the sake of compassion toward the rest, one should provide them with a livelihood.
Thus says Kātyāyana:
"But when a legitimate son (aurasa) has been born, they are declared to be entitled to a third share."
"But those of the same caste and those of different castes shall share in food and clothing" (Kātyāyana 857).

In the statement of Manu, the term *śeṣa* ("remainder"), and in the statement of Kātyāyana, the term *asavarṇa* ("of different caste"), refer to those of lower caste, because this is consistent with the single voice of Devala.
Manu states the division of a *kṣetraja* son born without formal authorization (*aniyoga*) along with the *aurasa* (legitimate) son:

"If there should be two sons, one legitimate (*aurasa*) and one born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), who are co-heirs, whatever paternal inheritance belongs to each, that he alone shall take, not the other.
(M 9.162) The meaning is this: whoever is born from whose seed, he shall take that man's wealth; the other, being born from another's seed, shall not take it. For this very reason, Nārada says:

If two sons born of two [different men] should dispute over the wealth of their mother, each shall take that which belonged to his own father, and not the other. That wealth which was given by the father belongs to the woman; her son begotten from that seed shall take that wealth, and no one else—let this suffice, for what need of further elaboration?
CHAPTER ELEVEN,

SECTION ONE <11.1.1> Now, regarding the wealth of one who has died without a son, commentators dispute one another due to the observation of mutually contradictory statements. <11.1.2> Thus says Bṛhaspati:
In the sacred tradition, in the treatises on law, and in worldly custom,
the wise have declared that a wife is half of one's body, sharing equally in the fruits of merit and demerit.
For him whose wife has not passed away, half of his body continues to live.
If one half of the body still lives, how could the other half receive the property?
[26.93] However, when there are agnates (sakulyas) who are blood relations on the father’s or mother’s side, the wife of a deceased man who leaves no son shall take his share. [26.94]

When her husband has died, a devoted wife shall take possession of his wealth—the Agnihotra fire and all else—along with his movable and immovable property, gold, base metals, grain, liquids, and clothing; this is the eternal law. [B 26.95]
Having taken it, he should cause the *śrāddha* for the monthly and half-monthly periods and so forth to be offered.

He should honor paternal uncles, teachers, daughters' sons, the husband's sister's son, maternal uncles, elders, guests, and women with offerings to the ancestors (*kavya*) and works of public utility (*pūrta*).
If her sapindas or kinsmen should obstruct her or seize her property,
the king shall punish them with the same penalty as for theft.

<11.1.3> Thus, by these seven statements, Bṛhaspati asserts that whatever wealth—whether immovable property, movable goods, gold, or the like—belongs to a husband who has died childless, all of it belongs to the wife alone, even when brothers of the whole blood, paternal uncles, daughters' sons, and others exist. He declares that those who oppose her right to take that wealth, or who seize it themselves, are to be punished like thieves; thereby, he utterly excludes the father, brothers, and other relatives from any claim to the inheritance when the wife is present.
<11.1.4> And likewise Yājñavalkya:
The wife, the daughters, the parents, the brothers, as well as their son, a kinsman of the same lineage, a relative, a pupil, and fellow students—
in the absence of each preceding one among these, the succeeding one is the heir to the wealth.
"This rule applies to all castes in the case of one who has died without a son" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.136).
By stating that each subsequent person has the right of succession in the absence of each preceding one, he declares that the wife alone has the primary right to the estate before anyone else.

Likewise, Viṣṇu states: "The wealth of one who dies without a son goes to the wife; in her absence, it goes to the daughter; in her absence, to the father; in his absence, to the mother; in her absence, to the brother; in his absence, to the brother’s son; in his absence, to a *sakulya* (a distant agnate); in his absence, to a *bandhu* (a cognate relative); in his absence, to the pupil; in his absence, to a fellow student; in his absence, with the exception of the property of a Brāhmaṇa, it goes to the King. By this sequence as well, the right of the wife alone to the inheritance is established first.

Nor should it be said that the mention of the wife is intended only for the purpose of authorizing her to receive a portion of the wealth sufficient for her maintenance; for it is improper to assume a difference in intention such that the word "wealth," heard only once, would refer to the whole in relation to brothers and others, yet refer only to a partial amount in relation to the wife. Therefore, the wife’s right of inheritance must be declared to concern the entire estate. Thus Vṛddha-Manu says: "A sonless widow, preserving the bed of her husband and remaining steadfast in her vows, shall herself offer his funeral cake and receive the entire share. [Vṛddha-Manu 92]

In the phrase "that lump" (*tat-piṇḍam*), the word "that" (*tat*) is understood from the preceding context. Since the word "that" refers back to the husband, the meaning is that the wife shall receive the husband's entire share, but not her own entire share; for it would be illogical to enjoin that she "shall receive" with reference to her own share, since this [text] is intended to make known the state of ownership over the husband's portion. Furthermore, it is not possible to make known the state of ownership regarding one's own share, because that is already known simply by the fact of its being one's own share.
Nor can it be said that the word "that" is intended to enjoin the act of taking; for the taking of one's own property is already established through natural inclination (*rāga*).

Nor should it be said that the statement is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), because that would result in [the injunction] having an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*). Furthermore, in the case of a restriction, there would also have to be the postulation of a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) and so forth.

And as for what was stated: "For when it is said that a son who is not blind and so forth shall not receive the entire share, does this mean the entire paternal share? Rather, it means his own entire share. Likewise, here too, "entire" is in reference to one's own share.

That is not so; for since there is no scriptural statement to the effect that "a son who is not blind and so forth shall receive the entire share," the analogy is untenable. Or, even if such a statement were to exist, nevertheless, because the injunction "he shall receive his own share" is untenable for the reason stated previously, it is proper to explain [the matter] solely with reference to the father’s share. <11.1.12> For this very reason, the sages everywhere indicate the relationship of one person to the wealth of another—such as the sons' right to the father's wealth, or the wife and others' right to the wealth of one who leaves no son—but they do not urge them to take their own respective shares.

Furthermore, as for the claim that a word functions as a relative term (*saṃbandhiśabda*) by bringing to mind its own correlate—just as it was stated that the word "mother" does not necessarily imply the biological mother—that too is incorrect. This is because such a term refers to a correlate that has not been explicitly mentioned. For instance, when it is said, "Bring the mother of Ḍittha," neither the mother of the person being addressed (*prayojya*) nor the mother of the person giving the command (*prayojaka*) is necessarily understood. Likewise here, since the correlate is already expressed by the word *tat* in the phrase *tatpiṇḍam*, how could the wife be required? Moreover, the impossibility of the injunction has already been stated previously.
<11.1.14> Therefore, Vṛddha-Manu teaches that the wife’s acquisition of the inheritance is indeed the taking of its entirety.

<11.1.15> Likewise, there are statements contrary to the wife’s entitlement, such as those of Śaṅkha-Likhita and Paiṭhīnasi-Yama: "The property of one who has died without a son goes to his brothers; in their absence, the parents shall receive it, or the wife, or the eldest [sister], or those of the same lineage, disciples, and fellow students.
[ŚL 293 = Pai 119] <11.1.16> Here, there is a contradiction: first the brother's right, then the parents' upon the brother's absence, and then the wife's entitlement upon the absence of those two.
<11.1.17> Likewise, Devala says:
"Then the uterine brothers shall divide the inheritance of one who dies without a son;
or the daughters of equal status, or even the father, if he is still living. [D 1570]
"The brother, the mother, and the wife are the heirs in that order;
in their absence, the kinsmen and the co-residents shall take [the property].
(D 1571) <11.1.18> Herein, there is a contradiction: the brother has the right of inheritance at the very beginning, while the wife has it at the very end of all.

<11.1.19> Here, some explain that the section concerning brothers has as its scope those who are undivided and not reunited (*avibhakta-asaṃsṛṣṭa*), whereas the section concerning the wife has as its scope those who are divided and not reunited (*vibhakta-asaṃsṛṣṭa*). <11.1.20> That contradicts Bṛhaspati, who says:
"Brothers who have been divided but have lived together again in one place out of mutual affection..."
Furthermore, when a division is made, there is no seniority among them.
If anyone should die or somehow renounce the world, his share is not lost; it is ordained for his uterine brother.
His sister, however, deserves to receive a share from that [inheritance];
this is the law for one who is childless and lacks both a wife and a father.
But as for those who have pooled their resources, whoever among them acquires wealth through learning, valor, or other such means—
To him who has arrived [as an heir], two shares must be given; the remaining [heirs] shall have equal shares.

(YDh 2.112) <11.1.21> Since the state of being reunited is mentioned both at the beginning and the conclusion here, that which is stated within those two boundaries is not sublated; rather, it is ordained that his share belongs to the uterine brother. (YDh 2.107cd)

This statement must be understood as referring to the case of reunited coparceners (*saṃsṛṣṭa*). In that context, the verse— "This is the law for one who is childless and for one who has neither wife nor father" (B 26.108cd)—establishes the entitlement of the reunited uterine brother in the absence of sons, daughters, wife, and father; how then can it be said to set aside the wife?

<11.1.22> Furthermore, as for the phrase "it is not lost": since there is a concern that [the property] might be lost when it is undivided and commingled—because it cannot be perceived separately once it has been mixed with the property of another brother—the statement "it is not lost" is appropriate. However, when the wealth is divided and uncommingled, and its state of being divided is clearly perceived, what room is there for a suspicion of loss?
Therefore, these statements refer exclusively to the case of commingled property.

<11.1.23> Furthermore, regarding the statements of Śaṅkha and others which establish the brother’s right of inheritance prior to that of the wife and so forth, does this refer specifically to a brother who was a *saṃsṛṣṭin* (one who lived in joint ownership), based on either a scriptural text or logical reasoning? In this regard, it cannot be based on a scriptural text, because there is no specific statement to that effect. As for the statements such as "the *saṃsṛṣṭin* [inherits] from the *saṃsṛṣṭin*," since they are intended to provide specific information at the occasion of establishing the brother's right of inheritance, it is impossible for them to have the purpose of establishing the brother's right of inheritance in general. <11.1.24> Moreover, since the statements of Bṛhaspati cited immediately above refer to those who were *saṃsṛṣṭins*, and since they establish the right of a uterine brother (*sodara-bhrātṛ*) in the absence of anyone from the son down to the daughter, the wife, and the father, it is more reasonable that these texts concern those who were not *saṃsṛṣṭins* (i.e., brothers who did not live in joint ownership), as they would otherwise contradict those [preceding] rules; they certainly do not concern those who were *saṃsṛṣṭins*.

<11.1.25> Now, this is stated according to logical reasoning (*nyāya*). For instance, in the case of joint ownership (*saṃsṛṣṭatva*), whatever wealth belongs to one brother belongs to the other as well. In that situation, although one's own ownership (*svatva*) is lost through death, because the ownership of the survivor has not departed from that [property], it remains his alone and not that of the wife; for by the death of the husband, the wife’s ownership is also destroyed. Just as, when sons and others exist, that wealth does not belong to the wife.

That is weak. For even if there is joint ownership (*saṃsṛṣṭatva*), what belongs to one does not necessarily belong to the other; rather, it refers to a portion that has not been specifically identified. That [ownership] belongs to both, but not in its entirety. As was stated at the very beginning, there is no evidence for the assumption of full ownership [over the whole]. Furthermore, the wife’s ownership over the husband’s wealth arises from marriage; and there is no evidence for the claim that this ownership perishes upon the husband’s death. However, when a son exists, the loss of the wife’s ownership is understood precisely from the scriptural injunction regarding the son’s right [to inherit].

If it is argued that here too the destruction of [the husband's] ownership is understood from the scriptural injunction regarding the brother’s right of succession, we say no; for the fact that this [injunction] pertains to a brother who was reunited (saṃsṛṣṭa) remains unestablished even now. Indeed, the scriptural rule concerning the brother’s right of succession would have a "reunited" subject matter only if the wife’s ownership were established to be destroyed by the death of a husband with whom she was reunited. But if that scriptural rule has such a subject matter, then there is a mutual dependency (itaretarāśrayatva): the destruction of the wife’s ownership depends on the rule, and the applicability of the rule depends on the destruction of her ownership.

<11.1.28> Furthermore, if the statements of Śaṅkha, Likhita, and others were intended to apply only to undivided and reunited coparceners, then the logical sequence would have to be stated as follows: "The wealth of one who is undivided or reunited goes to such brothers; but in the absence of such a person, the parents shall take it.
And thus, a dilemma would arise: should the parents who are divided and not reunited take the property, or those who are undivided and reunited?

The first alternative is not tenable; for since the rule "the wife and the daughters," etc., establishes that the property of parents who are undivided and unseparated is superseded by the wife, how could they have a right prior to her?

Nor is the second [alternative] tenable; because there is no dispute among anyone that even when undivided and unseparated brothers exist, the property must be taken by the undivided and unseparated father.

Furthermore, just as in the case of a father and a brother whose wealth is divided and not reunited—where, because of the scriptural statement of identity, "The self is indeed born as the son," due to the father's sovereignty over both the body and the wealth, and because the deceased becomes an enjoyer through *sapiṇḍana* at the two *piṇḍas* offered to his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, and because sons lack the right to offer the *pārvaṇa* *piṇḍas* while the father is alive—the father’s entitlement precedes that of the brothers; so too is it appropriate in the other case.

Alternatively, because there is no distinction between non-division and reunion, it is logical that the father and brother have equal entitlement, like those on a balance scale; it is not correct to say that the entitlement belongs to the father only in the absence of the brother. Furthermore, the dual number [in the phrase "the parents shall take"] would be inappropriate if it meant that the father and mother—both undivided and reunited—should take the property, since there can be neither division nor non-division with respect to the mother. For this very reason, there is also an absence of reunion [with the mother]. As Bṛhaspati says:
"He who, having been divided by his father or brother, dwells again in one place..."
"Or else, by affection for his father or brother, he is said to be reunited.

By this, he shows the following: for those very persons—such as a father, brother, or paternal uncle—who by birth have the state of non-separation regarding property acquired by their father or grandfather, they, having become separated, may through mutual affection, by the destruction of a previously made division, reunite in the form of a single household with a single house, thinking, "Whatever is your wealth is mine; whatever is my wealth is yours."

Furthermore, even among merchants, there is no status of "association" (*saṃsargitva*) merely by the physical contact of goods; nor does it exist among separated individuals merely through the contact of goods, in the absence of the aforementioned prior intention preceded by affection. Therefore, since the mere presence of association and non-separation cannot coexist with a mother, how is the contradiction regarding the entitlement to the existence of a brother residing in the mother to be resolved?

<11.1.31> Now, the matter is being considered by the wise. In this regard, from the statements of Viṣṇu and others, the entitlement of the wife is clearly understood to exist solely on account of the absence of a son. And this is logical: that the wealth of the deceased first belongs to the son, grandson, and great-grandson.
For thus say Manu and Viṣṇu:
"Because a son delivers his father from the hell named Put, [he is called a putra]."
Therefore, he was called "son" (putra) by the Self-Existent One himself. Likewise, Hārīta says:
"A hell named Punnāman has been proclaimed, and one whose lineage is severed is destined for that hell."
Because he indeed protects (*trāyate*) them there, he is therefore remembered as "son" (*putra*). Likewise, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"Having seen his son's face while living, the father becomes free from debt to the ancestors."
By producing such a son, he casts off that debt in him and attains heaven.

(ŚL 285) The Agnihotra sacrifice, the three Vedas, and sacrifices accompanied by hundreds of ritual fees do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of one who has fathered an eldest son. (ŚL 284)
On this point, Manu, Śaṅkha, Viṣṇu, Vasiṣṭha, and Hārīta [state]:
"Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains infinity;
and through the grandson of a son, one reaches the realm of the Sun."
Likewise, Yājñavalkya says:
"Through sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, one attains endless worlds and reaches heaven" (Y 1.78ab).

[11.1.32] Thus, since sons and others perform great services for their father, appropriate for the world beyond, from the very moment of his birth, that wealth—even though he is dead—benefits him for the sake of the sons and others through the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) according to the *pārvaṇa* rite; therefore, the ownership of the sons and others is established by logic and is declared in scripture.
Likewise, Manu also states that the connection with wealth arises precisely through the quality of being a benefactor:
"By the mere birth of the eldest son, a man becomes possessed of a son."
And since he is thus free from debt to his ancestors, he deserves to receive it.

<11.1.33> Because of the presentation of a reason with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*), and because in the section on the division of inheritance (*dāyabhāga*) the description of sons and others as being benefactors to their fathers and ancestors in various ways serves no other purpose, it is understood that the connection with wealth is according to Manu’s intention solely on account of that benefit. <11.1.34> For this very reason, the word "son" (*putra*) refers as far as the great-grandson (*prapautra*); for there is no distinction among those [descendants] ending with the great-grandson in their capacity to provide benefit through the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) according to the *pārvaṇa* rite. <11.1.35> Otherwise, it would be impossible to abandon the primary meaning of the word "son. Even if some statement indicating the entitlement of the grandson (*pautra*) could somehow be found, there is no separate mention of the great-grandson. <11.1.36> Therefore, since the great-grandson also possesses entitlement solely on account of providing benefit, the word "son" is used as an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).

<11.1.37> For this very reason, Baudhāyana says: "The great-grandfather, the grandfather, the father, oneself, uterine brothers, a son born of a woman of the same caste, a grandson, and a great-grandson—these, as long as they are undivided heirs, are called *sapiṇḍas*. Those whose inheritance has been divided are called *sakulyas*. When there are sons born of the body (*aṅgajas*), the property goes to them. In the absence of *sapiṇḍas*, the *sakulya* [inherits]. In his absence, the teacher, the pupil, or the officiating priest shall take it. In their absence, the king. [Bau 1.5.11.9–14]

<11.1.38> This is its meaning: because [the deceased] becomes an enjoyer through the *sapiṇḍana* rite in the three *piṇḍas* of the father and the others, and because the three [descendants], such as the son, offer that very *piṇḍa*, whoever was the giver of a *piṇḍa* while living becomes the enjoyer of that *piṇḍa* upon death through the *sapiṇḍana*.

This being so, the man situated in the middle—while living, was the giver of *piṇḍas* to his predecessors and, upon death, became their enjoyer; and while living, he was the recipient of the *piṇḍas* from his successors, and upon death, he became the enjoyer of the *piṇḍas* to be offered by the daughter’s sons (*dauhitra*) and others along with those deceased ancestors.

Therefore, those for whom this giver of the funeral ball (piṇḍa) is a relative, or who themselves are givers of that funeral ball, eat the inheritance in the form of the funeral ball as undivided; thus, they are "undivided heirs" (avibhaktadāyāda), namely, the sapindas.

However, for the fifth ancestor, the middlemost fifth is neither the giver of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) nor the eater of that rice-ball. Likewise, the fifth descendant below is neither the giver of the rice-ball to the middlemost nor the eater of that rice-ball. Therefore, because there is an absence of being a co-eater of the same rice-ball, the three ancestors starting from the great-great-grandfather and the three descendants starting from the great-grandson are called *sakulyas* (agnates), as they are divided heirs.

<11.1.39> This sapinda-relationship and sakulya-relationship have been stated for the purpose of determining the inheritance of property. <11.1.40> For this very reason, after Manu has declared: "Neither brothers nor fathers, but sons are the heirs to the father's estate" (M 9.185ab), when the question arises as to why this is so:
"Water-offerings should be made for three; the funeral cake (piṇḍa) proceeds for three.
The fourth is the giver of these; a fifth is not possible," so it has been said. [M 9.186]

<11.1.41> However, for the purpose of determining impurity (*aśauca*) and other matters, the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* specifies that even those who eat the remnants of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa-lepa-bhuj*) possess the status of a *sapiṇḍa* by virtue of being consumers of the remnants of the rice-balls offered by them. As it says: "The others who eat the remnants of the rice-balls are said to be three, beginning from the great-grandfather's grandfather; the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is the seventh among them."
Thus has this relationship extending to the seventh generation been declared by the sages;
the meaning is that it causes impurity (*aśauca*). For this very reason, it was also stated by Manu in the section on impurity:
"But the status of being a *sapiṇḍa* ceases with the seventh person."
"But the status of *samānodaka* [relatives] exists when the birth and name are unknown" (MDh 5.60).

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the rule "of the three" (MDh 5.61). However, in the absence of descendants up to the great-grandson (*prapautra*), the wife—being inferior to the sons and others because she performs acts for the benefit of her husband’s world beyond through vows and the like from the time of his widowhood—is the heir to the property in their absence. Thus says Vyāsa:
When her husband has died, a virtuous woman, remaining steadfast in the vow of celibacy,
should bathe every day and offer handfuls of water to her own husband;
she should also devotedly perform the worship of the deities before sunrise.
Having fasted, she should perform the constant worship of Viṣṇu;
she should give gifts to the foremost of Brahmins for the increase of merit,
and she should observe various fasts prescribed in the scriptures, O auspicious lady.

"O fair-faced one, a woman who is constantly devoted to dharma rescues both her husband and herself, even when he is situated in another world. (Vy 244) <11.1.44> Since, through such statements as these, it is heard that a wife also effects deliverance from hell, it follows that she who, being destitute of wealth, performs improper acts causes her husband to fall as well by the equalization of the fruits of merit and demerit; therefore, for that purpose, that wealth belongs to the former owner alone, and thus the wife’s ownership is logical.

<11.1.45> Therefore, in the statements concerning Śaṅkha and others, a construction involving an ellipsis must be made: "The wealth of one who has died without a son shall be taken by the eldest wife; in her absence, the parents shall take it; in their absence, it goes to the brothers. The phrase "in their absence" (*tadabhāve*), though read in the middle, connects both with the preceding clause "it goes to the brothers" and with the following clause "the parents shall take it," because there is no contradiction and because the underlying principle has already been stated.

<11.1.46> However, there is no assumption that the scope [of the rule] concerns those who are unmentioned, separated, or mixed. Therefore, without distinction and regardless of whether they are separated or otherwise, the entitlement of the wife to the husband’s entire estate as declared by Jitendriya is to be respected.

<11.1.47> And the status of being a "wife" (patnī) belongs first to one of the higher castes, because of the designation "the senior wife" (jyeṣṭhā patnī), since seniority follows the order of the castes. As Manu says:
"If twice-born men marry women both of their own caste and of other castes..."

"Among them, seniority, honor, and the right to wear the *veśa* (head-ornament) follow the order of their castes. [M 9.85] Therefore, even if she was married last, a wife of the same caste (*savarṇā*) is indeed the senior. She alone possesses the authority for participation in sacrifices and other rites, and thus holds the status of a true *patnī*. Likewise, Manu says:
"The service of the husband’s person and the daily performance of his religious duties..."

A woman of her own caste alone should perform these duties for all; never one of another caste. But he who, out of delusion, causes them to be performed by another woman while his own caste is available, is considered a Brāhmaṇa-Cāṇḍāla, exactly as previously described.

Furthermore, in the absence of a wife of the same caste (*savarṇā*), a wife of the next lower caste is permitted. Thus Viṣṇu states: "In the absence of a wife of the same caste, however, [he may take] one of the next lower caste in times of distress; but a twice-born man must never [take] a Śūdra woman. The phrase "he should perform his religious duties" is understood to follow here.

Therefore, for a Brāhmaṇa, the Brāhmaṇa woman is the wife; in her absence, even a Kṣatriya woman may be taken in times of distress, but never a Vaiśya or a Śūdra woman, even if she has been married. For a Kṣatriya, the Kṣatriya woman is the wife; in her absence, a Vaiśya woman may be taken because she belongs to the immediately following caste, but never a Śūdra woman. For a Vaiśya, only a Vaiśya woman is the wife, and never a Śūdra woman, since there is a prohibition against a Śūdra woman for any twice-born man (*dvija*).

By this very sequence of wives, the right to inherit property should be understood. Consequently, since women who have been married [to others] are not [one's own] wives, Nārada’s statement is made with reference to that.
If among brothers one should die without offspring or should renounce the world,
the remaining ones shall divide his property, excluding the wife’s separate property (strīdhana).
They shall also provide for the maintenance of his wives until the end of their lives.
If they protect the bed of their husband, they may take [the property] from the others as well;
likewise for him alone.
However, with the exception of a Brāhmaṇa, the king who is devoted to dharma [should act thus].
One should provide for the livelihood of their wives; this is recorded as the rule for inheritance.

There is no contradiction here, for it is understood that the provision of maintenance funds applies to those women who are not wives, whereas wives have the right to the entire estate. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati states:
"Those Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are sonless and deprived of both wives and brothers..."

The king shall take their wealth, for he is the lord of all. This indicates the king’s right to the property in the absence of a wife. As for the apparent contradiction with Nārada, who states that one should provide "maintenance" (*vartana*)—meaning the king should take all the wealth after giving a livelihood to their women—that conflict is to be resolved by distinguishing between the term *patnī* (wife) and *strī* (woman). For this very reason, the word *patnī* is used in the rules concerning the wife’s entitlement, while terms such as *strī*, *nārī*, and *bhāryā* are employed in the rules concerning maintenance.
<11.1.50> Furthermore, as for the statement of Devala:
"Then the uterine brothers shall divide the inheritance of one who dies without a son;
or likewise the daughters of equal status, or even the father, if he is still living. [D 1570]

"Those of the same caste (savarṇā), brothers, and the mother, as well as the wife, in that order; in their absence, the kinsmen (kulyāḥ) who live together shall take [the inheritance]. Here, "those of the same caste" refers to daughters. "Brothers of the same caste" is intended to mean stepbrothers, because since uterine brothers are already included by the specific term [used for them], an additional qualifier would be inappropriate.

Even there, the sequence of enumeration beginning with the uterine brothers and ending with the wife is not intended to establish the order of entitlement (*adhikāra*), as that would contradict Viṣṇu and others. Rather, its purpose is to indicate that they should take [the inheritance] according to the order stated by Viṣṇu and the rest. The use of the word "or" (*api vā*) in both instances—"daughters or even the father"—is merely to show a lack of insistence on the order of enumeration; for that [word "or"] is also applied elsewhere. Thus, Devala has shown that the order of mention—whether it be the uterine brothers, the daughters, or the father—is not fixed.

<11.1.51> Furthermore, as for what Bālaka has stated—that the statement of Śaṅkhāgni refers either to women of a different caste, or to young maidens, or to women who are unseparated or ununited—by thus explaining the meaning of the scripture in such an unsettled manner, he has merely revealed his own state of being a child; for due to this doubt, the performance of either one [of the options] would be impossible. <11.1.52> As for the description that the rule regarding "subsistence" (vartana) refers to unmarried or unconfined women, that too must be rejected on the grounds that it is intended for the favoring of legal wives (*dharmapatnī*), since the subject matter of the injunction for subsistence regarding women has already been demonstrated previously.

<11.1.53> Furthermore, even if there is a distinction regarding the wife based on whether she is of the same or a different caste (*savarṇa* or *asavarṇa*), how can the conflict regarding the entitlement of the parents and brothers be resolved? If it is argued that the distinction lies in their association or non-association with her, let that very distinction be all-pervasive. What is the use of postulating further distinctions such as the wife being of the same caste and so forth? We have already refuted this distinction in our previous detailed exposition. <11.1.54> Moreover, the distinction based on whether a brother is uterine or not is rejected by Bṛhaspati. Thus he says: "But while sapindas who are blood relations of the father and mother exist..."
"The wife of one who has died without a son shall take his share.

[B 26.94] "Sanābhayaḥ" means uterine brothers. This verse establishes the wife's connection to the property even when such brothers exist. Furthermore, from the word "tadbhāga" (his share), it is understood that the entire portion belonging to the husband is meant, and not merely a part of it.
Therefore, the legal principle of the scripture is exactly as we have demonstrated.

<11.1.56> A wife may indeed use her husband’s property, but she is not entitled to give it away, mortgage it, or sell it. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says: "A sonless widow, remaining under the protection of her elders and preserving her husband’s bed, may enjoy [the estate] until her death; after that, the heirs shall obtain it. [K 921]

<11.1.57> A woman who remains in her husband’s family with her father-in-law and other elders shall enjoy her husband’s property for as long as she lives. However, unlike her own *strīdhana*, she must not independently perform acts of giving, mortgaging, or selling. Upon her death, those heirs such as daughters who are entitled to the inheritance shall take it; the paternal kinsmen (*jñātayaḥ*) shall not. This is because the kinsmen are inferior to the daughters and others, and thus it is illogical for them to supersede them; indeed, it is the wife who supersedes them. For there is no difference between the prior non-existence and the subsequent destruction of their right of succession, and thus no superseding of the wife can logically occur.

<11.1.58> Nor should those entitled to the woman's property (strīdhana) take it, because they already have a specific jurisdiction over the woman's property; furthermore, since Kātyāyana has already stated the entitlements of those entitled to the woman's property through other statements, [this would result in] the fault of redundancy.

<11.1.59> Therefore, just as those subsequent heirs designated by the rule beginning with "the wife, the daughters... take the estate in the absence of each preceding one, so too should they take what remains after enjoyment even upon the extinction of the entitlement of a wife whose entitlement had previously arisen.
At that time, it is appropriate for daughters and others to have a right to the wealth, since they provide assistance to the deceased in comparison to others.
Likewise, in the *Dānadharma*:
"The inheritance of a woman from her own husband is traditionally held to have enjoyment as its fruit."
Women should never, under any circumstances, make an appropriation from the husband's inheritance.

Even regarding enjoyment, she is permitted to enjoy what is appropriate for maintaining the body—not merely by wearing fine garments and the like, but because she assists her husband by sustaining his own body. In this way, even acts such as giving away property for the sake of the husband’s funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*) and so forth are authorized. For this very reason, he states that women must not commit embezzlement; for embezzlement occurs when one makes use of wealth belonging to another. Therefore, even pledging (*ādhāna*) is permitted when there is an inability to subsist; and if even that is impossible, selling is also permitted, as the underlying principle remains the same.

<11.1.63> For the sake of performing the funeral rites for her husband, she should give property of corresponding value to her husband’s paternal uncle and other relatives. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:

"She should honor with offerings to the ancestors (kavya) and works of public utility (pūrta) her husband’s paternal uncle, preceptor, daughter’s son, sister’s son, and maternal uncle; as well as elders, guests, and women. [B 26.98]

The term *pitṛvya* (paternal uncle) refers to the husband’s *sapinda* relatives; the term *dauhitra* (daughter’s son) refers to the descendants of the husband’s daughter; the term *svasrīya* (sister’s son) refers to the descendants of the husband’s sister; and the term *mātula* (maternal uncle) refers to the family of the husband’s mother. One should give [the offerings] to these and others. However, while these [relatives] exist, one must not give to those in one’s own paternal or maternal families, as that would render the mention of the paternal uncle and others redundant. Nevertheless, with their permission, one may give even to one’s own paternal and maternal families. Regarding this, Nārada says:
"When the husband has died and she is without a son, the husband’s kin are the masters of the woman."
He is the master in matters of her employment, the protection of her interests, and her maintenance.
When the husband’s family has perished, when he is no longer among the living, and when there is no one left for refuge,
and when his paternal kinsmen (sapiṇḍas) are absent, the father’s side is the woman’s authority.

Regarding the application [of the rule] to giving and so forth: in the absence of a husband or son, she remains dependent upon her husband’s family. (11.1.65) And thus, since the daughter also acquires a right [to the estate], when she dies, those designated as heirs to the father's wealth shall take it, not those designated as heirs to the daughter's wealth. (11.1.66) Furthermore, from the husband's wealth, a fourth part must be given by the wife to the daughter for the purpose of her marriage; since that gift is established as being for the sons alone, the giving to the wife and others is understood through the logic of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpika*).
<11.1.67> Thus concludes the section on the wife’s entitlement.
Section Two:
<11.2.1> In the absence of a wife, the daughter has the entitlement. On this point, Manu and Nārada [state]:
"Just as one's own self, so is a son; a daughter is equal to a son.
While she lives as one's very self, how could another take away the wealth?
Thus Nārada distinguishes the daughter.
"In the absence of a son, however, the daughter [is the heir], because an equal lineage is observed;
for both the son and the daughter are the continuers of the father’s lineage.

Regarding the daughter’s entitlement, the observation of lineage is stated as the reason. And lineage is intended to be that which offers the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*); for one who does not offer the funeral cake provides no benefit, and thus there is no distinction between such a person and another who lacks a lineage altogether.

<11.2.2> And the daughter’s son (*dauhitra*) is the giver of that funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), neither is it her son nor her daughter; for the succession of the *piṇḍas* ends with him. <11.2.3> Therefore, the view of Dīkṣita—that a woman who has sons or whose sons are expected is the rightful heir, whereas one whose sons are lost due to widowhood, barrenness, or having given birth only to daughters is not an heir at all—is worthy of respect.

<11.2.4> In that regard, first of all, the maiden alone is the heir to the father's wealth. As Parāśara states: "The daughter who is unmarried shall take the inheritance of one who has died without a son; in her absence, the married [daughter] shall do so. The term "married" refers to the specific distinctions previously mentioned. <11.2.5> Likewise, Devala says:
"And for the maidens, the wealth for the wedding should be given from the paternal property."

"The daughter of one who has no son shall, being of her own [caste] and born of lawful wedlock, inherit like a son. [D 1598] The term *putrikā* (appointed daughter) is an indicator for [any] son. "Of her own" means of the same caste (*savarṇā*). "Born of lawful wedlock" means legitimate (*aurasī*). This is appropriate; for it is heard in scripture that if a maiden who has not been married sees her menses, her father and others fall into hell in the absence of wealth. Vasiṣṭha says this:

"As long as the seasons touch a maiden—even if she is desirous and being solicited by a suitable suitor—for that many beings have been killed by those two, the mother and father; such is the declaration of Dharma.

Likewise, Paiṭhīnasi states: "She should be given away while her breasts have not yet emerged. If she becomes subject to the seasons (menstruating), then both the giver and the receiver fall into hell, and the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather are reborn in excrement. Therefore, she should be given away while still a *nagnikā* (pre-pubertal)."

<11.2.7> Therefore, because she rescues her father and other relatives from hell by being employed in marriage, and because she is beneficial even through her son to those who have married her, wealth for that purpose belongs solely to the master [the husband]; thus, in the absence of a wife, it is logical that ownership belongs to the daughter. <11.2.8> When ownership rests with the daughter, the right belongs to one who has a son expected or who already has a son. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"A suitable girl, wedded to a suitable man, virtuous, and devoted to service..."
Whether she has borne children or not, she is the one who inherits the father’s wealth.

"Of similar kind" means of the same caste as the father. The phrase "married by one of her own kind" is intended to exclude marriages with women of higher or lower castes; for it is prohibited to perform *śrāddha* rites for maternal grandfathers and others of higher or lower castes on behalf of a son born from a mother married to a man of a higher or lower caste. However, in the case of a woman married to a man of her own caste, she benefits the father through her sons.

<11.2.10> However, because the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*) provides an even greater benefit—just like a biological son—it follows that through him the appointed daughter is equal to a biological son; thus, the right to inherit the property is equal for both the appointed daughter and the biological son. But as for an unmarried daughter who has no [appointed] son, her capacity to provide benefit occurs only through her own son, who provides less benefit than a son born to another; therefore, it is logical that the right to inherit belongs only when there is an absence of all heirs down to the unmarried daughter. <11.2.11> Nor should it be argued: "In that case, let the primary right belong only to one who already has a son; but in his absence, let it belong to one who is likely to have a son."

Because, otherwise, the daughter’s son born after her would fall into a state of non-entitlement; and that is not logical, since there is no difference in the benefit conferred upon both by virtue of being a daughter’s son (*dauhitra*). <11.2.12> By demonstrating her lifelong devotion to serving her husband as a sign of her widowhood, he shows that she possesses the potential for bearing sons. <11.2.13> The word "she" (*sā*) refers back to the daughter mentioned in the preceding statement. Thus, by means of the qualifiers such as "a similar [woman] wedded to a similar [man]," he demonstrates that it is not merely by being a daughter that she has the right to her father's wealth. <11.2.14> Otherwise—
"A daughter arises from every limb of men like a son;
how then could another man take her father’s property?

Since the right of the daughter has already been stated by this verse, to state it again in the passage beginning with "a similar [daughter] wedded by a similar [husband]" would be redundant. However, when a general rule has already been established, stating a specific exception is certainly not redundant.

<11.2.15> Precisely because a daughter has a right to her father’s wealth by virtue of being the giver of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) through her own son, for that very reason, when a *putrikā* (appointed daughter) who has already established a connection with her father’s wealth subsequently dies—whether due to barrenness or because her husband is incapable of procreation resulting in the failure to produce a son—that wealth does not go to the husband. As Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “The husband does not deserve the property of a deceased *putrikā* who is childless” [ŚL 295]. Likewise, Paiṭhīnasi says: “But when a *putrikā* has died, the husband does not deserve the property.”
"In the case of a daughter who is childless, or of a maiden, it should be taken by her sister, or by another.

[Pai 120] Therefore, that wealth is to be taken by the maiden sister, or by another sister who has sons or whose son is expected. Consequently, within the section concerning women, there is an exclusion of the authority of others.
As for the statement of Manu:
"But if a putrikā dies without having borne a son,
her husband shall take that wealth without hesitation. This should be understood to apply to the death of a putrikā who either has no son at all or whose son has died.
<11.2.17> Bṛhaspati restates that the offering of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) alone is the single basis for both [the mother and the maternal grandfather]:
"Just as she has ownership over the father's wealth even when her own kinsmen are present, so too does her son have a right to the wealth of his mother and maternal grandfather. [B 26.133]

Just as by that very offering of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) given to the daughter's son, the daughter becomes the heir to her father’s wealth, so too by that same offering of the cake, the daughter’s son also becomes the owner of his maternal grandfather’s wealth, even when the father and other relatives are present.
This statement is not intended to refer to the son of a woman who has no son (*aputrakā*). For it is said:
"Whether she has borne a son or not, she shall indeed take the wealth of her father who has no son" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.132cd).

Because of the reference by the word "her" (*tasyāḥ*) and "her son" (*tatsutaḥ*), it is precisely the daughter who was both appointed and unappointed—mentioned in this statement—who is intended; for, due to proximity rather than anything else, it is logical that she alone is referred to, and not that she should be excluded. For this very reason, Manu says:
"For the daughter's son shall take the entire inheritance of his father who has no [other] sons."
He himself should offer two funeral cakes (piṇḍas), one to his father and one to his maternal grandfather.
In this world, there is no difference between a son’s son and a daughter’s son according to the law,
for both their parents were produced from his own body.

He points to the birth of a daughter from the body of her maternal grandfather as the reason for the son of that daughter (the *dauhitra*) having a right to the inheritance; however, this does not refer to the formal act of designating a daughter (*putrikā-karaṇa*). Otherwise, he would have specified that very act.
To this effect, the same author has stated explicitly:
"Whether she has been formally designated or not, the son whom she bears to a husband of equal status..."

"The grandson (pautrī) [is the son] of the maternal grandfather; through him, he should offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) and inherit the wealth. [M 9.136] This declares the entitlement even of a grandson born of a daughter who has not been formally appointed as a *putrikā*. Furthermore, in the *smṛtis*, the term *dauhitra* invariably refers to one other than the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*). Thus Baudhāyana states: "Having accepted a daughter as a *mātā* (mother), [the son born of her is] the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*); any other is a *dauhitra*. [Bau 2.2.3.15] The word "one should know" (*vidyāt*) is understood to follow.

<11.2.22> For this very reason, Bhojadeva also, having cited Bṛhaspati in the section concerning the rights of the daughter’s son regarding what has been done and what has not been done, recorded the statement: "Just as there is ownership over the father's wealth [so it is for the daughter’s son]. <11.2.23> Likewise, Govindarāja also, in his commentary on Manu, stated: "In a lineage where there is neither a son nor a grandson, the daughter’s sons shall obtain the wealth."
"For regarding the ancestral offerings (svadhākāra) of the ancestors, the son's sons and the daughter's sons are equal.
By the force of this statement of Viṣṇu, it is shown that the daughter's son has a right [to the inheritance] even prior to the married daughter.

<11.2.24> And that [view] is not pleasing to us, because it contradicts such statements as "a similar [son] having married a similar [daughter]. <11.2.25> Rather, the right of the daughter's son (*dauhitra*) arises precisely from the absence of a daughter of the aforementioned description, even though the father and others exist. This is because of the injunction that he "exists in the same manner" as the daughter (*duhitṛvat*), and because of the mention of "his son too" (*tatsuto 'pi*) as being for the sake of inclusion (*apy-arthatayā*). Since this indicates the subordinate status of the daughter's son, it is established that the daughter's son has the right of inheritance immediately after the daughter.

By the statement "even though kinsmen exist," it is indicated that the entitlement of the parents is set aside by the daughter and the daughter's son, even if the husband is otherwise eligible in the absence of a wife. Since there is no other sublater [of this rule], the entitlement of the parents is thus implied. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati immediately follows:

"In their absence, however, the brothers, the sons of the brothers, the uterine siblings, the *sakulyas*, the distant relatives (*bāndhavas*), the pupils, and those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriyas*) are entitled to the wealth. (B 26.134)

By the word "that" (tat), there is a reference to the daughter's son and the parents who have been previously indicated; therefore, in their absence, the right of succession belongs to the brothers and the others. As for the statement of Bālaka:
"The wife, the daughters, the parents, and likewise the brothers... [Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.135ab].

The claim that, due to such fixed sequence, the right of the daughter’s son (*dauhitra*) belongs only to those below [the daughter] is merely the speech of a fool, as it contradicts Bṛhaspati. This is because the plural form of the word *duhitṛ* (daughter) itself indicates the inclusion of the unmarried daughter, the married daughter, and the daughter’s son; thus, there is no contradiction in the order.

Just as in the phrase "of one who has departed this world and is sonless," the word *putra* refers to [descendants] up to the great-grandson (*prapautra*) because there is no difference in their capacity to offer the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), so too, since the daughter’s son also offers the funeral cake, the word *duhitṛ* extends up to him.
Or, for example:

"In the absence of a son, however, the daughter [inherits], because an equal lineage is observed" (N 13.50ab). In this passage, the word "son" (*putra*) refers to everything up to and including the wife. Otherwise, the plural form "daughters" (*duhitaraḥ*) would be meaningless; for just as in the case of "the wife and her son" (*patnī tatsuta*), one would have used the singular alone. We shall explain later that the plural form in "brothers" (*bhrātaraḥ*) also possesses its own meaningful purpose.

<11.2.28> Furthermore, because there is a fixed sequence beginning with the father and ending with the king, it must be stated that in the absence of the king, the daughter's son (dauhitraka) holds the right of succession. Nor could it ever be maintained that the daughter's son has no right at all in the absence of the king.

<11.2.29> Therefore, the determination of the daughter's son's right of succession in the absence of a daughter, as formulated by Viśvarūpa, Jitendriya, Bhojadeva, and Govindarāja, is to be respected.

Furthermore, when a girl who has already acquired a legal right [to her father's property] dies after being married, then that wealth belongs to those—such as the husband and others—to whom it was assigned in the case of her death while her right had not yet arisen; and even in the absence of one whose right had arisen, the wealth belongs to those same persons. It does not, however, belong to her husband or others, because that [rule] pertains specifically to the woman’s separate property (*strīdhana*).

By the statement, "One may enjoy [the property] until death with forbearance," it is shown that in the absence of a wife who has acquired rights (*jātādhikārā*), daughters and others who receive the inheritance from the former owner of the wealth—provided they are not wives who have not yet acquired rights (*anutpannādhikāra*)—possess the right of succession. Thus, the fact that the daughter and granddaughter hold a right subsequent to the wife is established by the logic of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpanyāya*). Alternatively, the term "wife" (*patnī*) is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*); the intended meaning is that this principle should be understood as applying to all women in general who possess the right of succession. This concludes the section on the right of the daughter and granddaughter. Section Three.

<11.3.1> In the absence of a daughter’s son, the right belongs to the father, not to the mother, nor to both parents simultaneously; for this would contradict the statement of Viṣṇu: "In his absence, it goes to the father; in his absence, it goes to the mother" [ViDh 17.6–7]. <11.3.2> As for the statement of Manu: "The mother shall obtain the inheritance of a son who dies without offspring..."
"And when the mother has also passed away, the father's mother shall take the wealth.
And as for the statement of Bṛhaspati:
"In the case of one who has died childless, being deprived of both wife and son..."
"The mother should be known as the heir to the estate, or the brother with her permission.

This is to be understood as applying in the absence of [heirs] ending with the father. And this is logical: since the father’s right of succession precedes that of the maternal grandfather and the mother, the father is junior to the daughter's son (*dauhitra*)—because the daughter's son gives two *piṇḍas* that are to be enjoyed by the deceased, whereas the father is merely a giver of two *piṇḍas* that are to be enjoyed by the deceased; however, [the father is senior] to the mother and others because he gives two *piṇḍas* that are to be enjoyed by the deceased.

And because of the strength derived from the superiority understood through the statement of Manu: "Of the seed and the womb, the seed is said to be superior" (M 9.35ab), and because in the phrase "the parents," the paternal sequence alone is understood; for, from the nominal stem *pitṛ* ("father"), the father is first understood, and only subsequently is the mother understood by means of the force of the dual number and the assumption of *ekaśeṣa* (elliptical retention of one).

<11.3.5> Therefore, the cognition of sequence is pervaded by the designation of sequence. Since that [designation] is absent, the cognition of sequence is also absent; thus, the inference [based on this] is invalid. It must be rejected because the pervader's absence is unestablished and because it contradicts the words of Viṣṇu.
<11.3.6> Thus ends the section on the father’s authority.
Section Four.

<11.4.1> In the absence of the father, the mother has the right [to the inheritance]. This follows from the scriptural statement of Viṣṇu: "In his absence, it goes to the mother" (ViDh 17.7), which occurs immediately after the section on the father's rights. <11.4.2> And this is logical; because she has performed a service through the bearing and nourishing of the fetus, the repayment of that service must necessarily be made. <11.4.3> Therefore, the claim that the mother’s right comes before the father’s simply because her dignity exceeds that of the father is to be rejected. If the superiority of dignity were the cause for the connection with property, [the following would ensue]:...

Since it is stated, "Of the progenitor and the giver of the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is more venerable" (MDh 9.146ab), the teacher’s right of succession arises prior to that of the father; and because, even when a younger brother or a nephew exists, the right of succession would otherwise fall to paternal uncles and others.

Thus, by asserting that the mother’s right of succession occurs before the deceased’s paternal line and after the father, it is indicated that the grandmother’s right to the property occurs before the grandfather’s lineage and after the grandfather. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the sequence [of the verse]: "The parents, and likewise the brothers... (MDh 9.217).
In this very regard, Manu states that even when the mother has passed away, the father’s mother shall take the wealth. [M 9.217cd]

The meaning is: "when [the inheritance] has been taken by one who possesses a lineage. The word *api* ("also") and the particle *ca* ("and") are to be construed with both [clauses]. Therefore, when the mother has taken [the inheritance], one may also take it from the paternal grandmother; how much more so from brothers and the rest? By the word *api*, brothers and the others are indicated as being included up to the paternal grandmother. Thus, this is the sense of the statement: after those ending with the daughter's son (*dauhitra*)—that is, beyond the deceased’s own lineage—the parents have the right of succession according to the previously stated order. Consequently, the right of the paternal grandfather and great-grandfather prior to one's own lineage is demonstrated by this very rule.

For this very reason, since Yājñavalkya did not mention the entitlement of the paternal grandfather and great-grandfather even before that of the paternal uncle and others—by demonstrating the entitlement of the mother alone—he did not state it separately.
Thus ends the section on the entitlement of the mother.
Section Five.

In the absence of the mother, the property goes to the brother; for after stating "it goes to the mother," the statement of Viṣṇu says, "in her absence, it goes to the brother" (Vi 17.8). Here, the word "that" refers back to the mother's share. Furthermore, in the verse "the parents and likewise the brothers" (Yājñavalkya 2.135b), it is understood that the brother has the right of inheritance upon the absence of both parents.

<11.5.2> Nor should it be argued that the brother's son is entitled immediately after the mother in the same manner as the brothers, on the grounds that "the son of the brother" follows from the fact that "the brothers" are so designated; for this would contradict Viṣṇu’s statement: "It goes to the brothers; in their absence, it goes to the brother's son. Here, the word "that" (tat) refers back to the brother.

<11.5.3> And this is logical: because [the son] benefits his mother by offering the three funeral cakes (piṇḍas) intended for the deceased father and the other two ancestors; likewise, because he takes her place by offering the three funeral cakes intended for the maternal grandfather and others. Since such a [son] is stronger than a brother’s son or similar relatives, and since the brother is rooted in the mother, it is proper that the right of succession belongs only to those who follow after the mother.

<11.5.4> Furthermore, why is the word *tathā* not connected with the brother alone? For if it were so, then just as there are two parents, so too would there be brothers; thus, the entitlement (*adhikāra*) of the parents and the brothers would be equal.
<11.5.5> Therefore, this objection must be refuted by means of the contradiction with the statement of Viṣṇu, and that [contradiction] is the same elsewhere as well. Thus says Manu:
"The father shall take the inheritance of one who has no son, or the brothers themselves. [M 9.185cd]
He states that only the brothers themselves shall take [the inheritance], and not the brother’s son, who lacks the right.

Furthermore, why is the right of a brother’s son whose father is still living not accepted? There is no other reason for this than the fact that, because he does not offer the *piṇḍa* (funerary cake) while his father lives, he provides no benefit. If that is the case, then since a brother’s son whose father is dead likewise lacks an equal degree of benefit, how can he have an equal right? For this very reason, Devala says:
"Then the uterine brothers shall divide the estate of one who has no sons."

"Daughters are equal, as are the father while still living; likewise, brothers of the same caste, the mother, and the wife," according to this sequence— since the son of a brother is not mentioned in this chain of succession beginning with the wife, the daughter of the same caste, the father, the mother, and ending with the uterine brother and the half-brother, it is stated that the sons of a brother have no right of inheritance except in the absence of all those preceding the half-brother.

<11.5.7> Furthermore, the scriptural remembrance of his status as a son in the verse, "All those [deceased ancestors] by that son" (M 9.182c), is for the purpose of his offering the funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍa*). And it is for the purpose of his entitlement to the wealth in the absence of a brother, because otherwise there would be a contradiction with the previously cited statement; for [if he were not entitled], he would not have been established as such prior to the brothers.
<11.5.8> Therefore, the entitlement belongs first and foremost to the brother alone.

<11.5.9> Even there, first of all, it belongs to the uterine brother alone. As it has been stated: "But for a uterine brother, the uterine brother" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.138b). Since it was said "likewise for brothers" at the occasion of discussing the brother's right of inheritance, the meaning is that the uterine brother should take [the property] first. In his absence, however, it belongs to the half-brother, because he too possesses the meaning of the word "brother" by virtue of originating from the same source. <11.5.10> And so it is said: "The reunited coparcener shall take the share of the reunited coparcener; likewise, the uterine brother [takes the share] of the uterine brother. He shall give and take the share for one who is born and for one who has died" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.138).

This statement of Yājñavalkya also demonstrates that the term *bhrātṛ* (brother) applies to both uterine and non-uterine brothers. Otherwise, if the term applied to the uterine brother alone, the phrase "but the uterine [brother]" would not need to be specified again, since the sense of "uterine" would already be understood from the word *bhrātṛ* itself.

Therefore, by the expression "parents and brothers," the eligibility of both uterine and non-uterine brothers is shown; however, by the specific mention of the "uterine," the priority of the uterine brother's claim is indicated.

<11.5.12> Furthermore, because a half-brother (*sāpatna*) is inferior to a uterine brother (*sodara*)—since the latter offers the three *piṇḍas* beginning with the father, which are to be enjoyed by the deceased, while the former offers only the two *piṇḍas* to be enjoyed by the deceased—and because the uterine brother’s son is stronger than the half-brother due to his superior benefit in offering the three *piṇḍas* to be enjoyed by the deceased (rather than just two), the entitlement belongs to the middle [uterine brother] alone; this very view stated by Śrīkara and Viśvarūpa is what should be respected.
<11.5.13> In this regard, when there arises the question of whether or not even a half-brother who is reunited (*saṃsṛṣṭin*) is inferior to a uterine brother, Yājñavalkya says:

But a uterine brother who is a *saṃsṛṣṭin* (one who has reunited) shall take the wealth; one who is not uterine shall not take it. And even one who is not a *saṃsṛṣṭin* may take it, but one born of a different mother who is a *saṃsṛṣṭin* shall not. [Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.139] The meaning of this is as follows: First, a uterine brother who is a *saṃsṛṣṭin* shall take [the inheritance]. It is not merely anyone who is not uterine who may do so. Regarding the question of whether he takes it first by setting aside his uterine brother or together with him, the second half of the verse provides the answer: "Even one who is not a *saṃsṛṣṭin*—that is, a uterine brother—may take it. The term "uterine brother" (*sodara*) is understood to carry over from the previous line. It is not only one born of a different mother who is a *saṃsṛṣṭin* who may take it.

Or rather, the term *saṃsṛṣṭa* (one who has reunited) itself denotes a uterine brother (*sodara*). For this very reason, the statement of Bṛhad-Yājñavalkya—"a uterine brother, not one born of another mother"—was cited by Jitendriya. And in that context, the word "reunited" (*saṃsṛṣṭī*) from the first half of the verse is understood to carry over.
