Therefore, the meaning is that not only a reunited uterine brother alone shall take [the property], but even a non-reunited uterine brother may do so. Consequently, the inheritance should be divided and taken by both the non-reunited uterine brother and the reunited non-uterine brother. It is for this reason that he employed the particle *api* (even/also). Furthermore, as for what was stated by Śrīkaramiśra—

Regarding the rule "the *saṃsṛṣṭin* [inherits] from the *saṃsṛṣṭin*," since it refers exclusively to a non-uterine brother who is a *saṃsṛṣṭin*, it is independent [of other rules]. Likewise, regarding the rule "the uterine brother [inherits] from the uterine brother," since it refers exclusively to a uterine brother who is a *saṃsṛṣṭin*, it is also independent. When both [rules] would apply—namely, when there is a non-uterine brother who is a *saṃsṛṣṭin* and a uterine brother who is not a *saṃsṛṣṭin*—if both were to operate simultaneously, then both would be prescriptive with mutual dependence. However, it is not appropriate for a single [rule] to be both dependent and independent in its prescriptiveness, as this would result in an inconsistency in the injunction (*vidhivaiṣamya*).

As has been shown in the section concerning the two [types of fires] being led forward (*praṇayana*), there would be an application of the rule "the altar prescribed for the four joints (*parvan*) [is used]" and the rule "but for one who is uterine, [it is] uterine" during two of those joints. In that case, since neither rule would apply when there is a non-uterine brother who is a co-heir (*saṃsṛṣṭin*) and a uterine brother who is not a co-heir, no one at all would take that wealth; thus, the matter falls into an undesirable conclusion.

"Therefore, regarding the rule *'but the reunited [inherits] from the reunited'* (*saṃsṛṣṭinas tu saṃsṛṣṭī*), since the share of a reunited kinsman would generally apply to the reunited property, the statement *'but a uterine brother [inherits] from a uterine brother'* (*sodarasya tu sodaraḥ*) is intended as an exception to that. And thus, even for a reunited kinsman who is not uterine, there is no entitlement when a uterine brother exists; rather, the division belongs exclusively to the uterine brother, whether he was reunited at the time of partition or not—this is the final conclusion. That is inconsistent. For when two rules each apply individually to both cases, there is no inconsistency in the injunction merely by virtue of their simultaneous application to one and the same case.

<11.5.18> When there is a simultaneous failure of both the Udgātṛ and the Pratihartṛ, two scriptural injunctions—one prescribing the giving away of all one's property (*sarvasva*) and the other prescribing the absence of such gifts (*adakṣiṇya*)—which operate independently, neither injunction would apply because of the incompatibility of their prescriptions (*vidhivairūpyāt*).

<11.5.19> Similarly, regarding the two rules—"one should touch the *paurṇamāsī* [offering] with the *caturhotṛ* formula" and "one should touch the *amāvāsyā* [offering] with the *pañcahotṛ* formula"—when these two rules, which apply respectively to the *upaṃśuyāja* and the *agnīṣomīya*, and to the curd for Indra and the milk for Indra, were to apply simultaneously to the *āgneya* offering, neither would apply due to the resulting disparity in the prescriptions.

Therefore, the fact that in some cases there is an injunction as if it were eternal, independent of sublation, while in other cases it depends upon the sublation of another injunction, constitutes the characteristic of heterogeneity (*vairūpya*).

For instance, the prohibition "one should not sow in the vicinity" (upātra vapanti) is dependent upon the injunction regarding the altar (*vedi*); without subverting that injunction, the prohibition itself would not even exist. Thus, its formulation is dependent upon the subversion of the injunction for the altar. Furthermore, its subversion does not occur as if it were merely obligatory (*nityavat*). If that were the case, the prohibition would be purposeless, since the non-construction of the altar would already be established even without the prohibition. Consequently, the injunction for the altar also exists as an injunction whose status is dependent upon the subversion of the prohibitory injunction. However, on the two [specific] lunar days (*parvan*), it is independent; otherwise, there would be a discrepancy in the nature of the injunctions and an option (*vikalpa*) would result. But in the case of what is prompted by desire (*rāgaprāpta*), the subversion occurs as if it were obligatory, because the occasional non-performance of such an act would otherwise be established even without a prohibition.
<11.5.21> For this very reason, there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the taking or not taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup.

<11.5.22> As for those who say—"Since a prohibition presupposes a prior application, the injunction does not sublate the cause [of the application]; therefore, by this principle, there is an option"—in their view, there would have to be an option even in cases such as "He does not make those two nooses," and in prohibitions based on worldly inclination (*rāga*).

Furthermore, since that which possesses a cause is incapable of subverting its own cause, how could there be subversion even in the case of the [prohibitory] position, given the inequality of their strength? If it is argued that this is the very nature of the prohibition—that it uproots its own cause—then it would uproot it at all times, because the prior application (*prāpti*) itself is weak.

<11.5.24> As for those who say: "This is a prohibition against obtaining [the object] by chance, but not a prohibition of what is obtained through a scriptural injunction (vidhi)," that is the speech of one who is utterly ignorant. For it is impossible to simultaneously enjoin the taking [of the object] according to an injunction and prohibit the taking [of it] contrary to an injunction; this would result in the absence of any alternative option (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, since there is no possibility of obtaining [the object] by chance when it serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), the prohibition could not itself serve the purpose of the sacrifice.
<11.5.25> Therefore, the alternative option exists precisely according to the reasoning stated by us. Let it be so; what is the use of further elaboration?

Furthermore, that which you yourself have described—namely, that when the rule "the reunited [inherits] from the reunited" establishes a connection with the wealth for a half-brother who is reunited, the statement "but the uterine [inherits] from the uterine" is intended as an exception to that—is also incorrect. For in this very same context, since the rule "but the uterine [inherits] from the uterine" would likewise establish a connection with the wealth for the uterine brother, it is possible that the rule regarding the "reunited" is intended as an exception to that; thus, there is no decisive reason [to prefer one over the other].

Furthermore, the statement "anyodarya" (one born of a different womb), which was explained as being for the purpose of clarifying the rule "the reunited [heir] shall take the property of the reunited," is also highly improper. This is because the intended meaning is already obtained from the very mention of "anyodarya," which would render the term "saṃsṛṣṭinaḥ" (of the reunited) redundant.

<11.5.28> Furthermore, regarding the statement "but a half-brother who is a *saṃsṛṣṭin*," this is its meaning: a half-brother who is a *saṃsṛṣṭin* shall not take the wealth of the other half-brother; rather, even if he is not a *saṃsṛṣṭin*, by the connection with the term "uterine" (*sodara*), he alone—the uterine brother—shall take it. It has been explained that even one who is a *saṃsṛṣṭin* shall not take [it] if he is born of another mother. That too is not correct, because the term "half-brother" (*anyodarya*) is redundant in the first half-verse. Likewise, in the second half-verse as well, it would result in the term "born of another mother" (*nānyamātṛja*) being meaningless. Moreover, the particle *api* is observed to have the sense of the restrictive particle *eva*.

<11.5.29> Furthermore, since the mention of the "uterine brother" (*sodara*) has been explained as being for the purpose of setting aside the "non-uterine brother" (*asodara*) who is a co-heir (*saṃsṛṣṭin*), there would be no application [of the rule] for two brothers—one uterine and one non-uterine—who are both not co-heirs; consequently, their entitlement would either be exactly equal or there would be no entitlement for anyone at all. <11.5.30> If, on the other hand, the very same mention of the "uterine brother" were to apply here as well, then in one case it would depend upon the sublation of the mention of "co-heir," while in the other it would be independent of such sublation; thus, you yourselves would incur a discrepancy in the injunction (*vidhivairūpya*). This is just as it was stated regarding the altar (*vedi*) prescribed for the *Soma* sacrifice: that which is prescribed for the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites [is seen] to involve a sublation of the altar obtained through extension (*atideśa*), whereas in other cases it occurs without sublation; because of this discrepancy, it was said that "that [rule] should be understood as applying to those [sacrifices] that do not possess an altar."

In this view, however, there is no inconsistency with the injunction even according to the opinion of Śrīkara. This is because the two statements concerning the *saṃsṛṣṭin* (one reunited) and the *sodara* (uterine brother) each have their own distinct scope; and because the statement regarding the *anyodarya* (half-brother) is intended to establish that both the uterine brother who is not reunited and the half-brother who is reunited possess equal rights. To explain: the meaning of the first half-verse is that "the half-brother (*anyodarya*), if he is reunited (*saṃsṛṣṭin*), shall take the property even when a uterine brother (*sodara*) exists who is not reunited; the half-brother shall not take it even if he is not reunited. In response to the question—what then of the uterine brother at that time? Should he not take it at all?—the answer is given by the second half-verse: "Even if not reunited, the uterine brother (*sodara*) shall take [it]. The word "uterine" (*sodara*) is supplied from the previous context. The meaning is that it is not only the half-brother born of another mother who is reunited who takes it, but rather that the inheritance must be divided between both.
<11.5.32> Likewise, Manu also demonstrates this very point:
"The uterine brothers, having come together and assembled, shall divide it equally; as shall those brothers who are reunited, and the uterine sisters. (M 9.212)

Regarding the statement, "For uterine [brothers] alone, [the term] 'uterine' applies; and for non-uterine [brothers], if they are reunited, [the term] 'reunited' applies," since the mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) is understood from the plural-ending word itself, it is appropriate that the words "having come together" (*sametya*) and "united" (*sahitāḥ*) serve solely to express the conjunction of both groups, as otherwise they would be redundant. Therefore, the claim that "there is no hearing of the mutual conjunction of both" is an unhearted utterance. Furthermore, because the particle *ca* is heard in the phrase "and those who... (*ye ca*), and because the copulative compound (*dvandva*) is also heard in the sense of *ca*, the assertion that there is no hearing of mutual conjunction implies that even the copulative compound does not have that as its meaning.

<11.5.34> Therefore, when both uterine and non-uterine brothers exist, the inheritance belongs to the uterine brothers alone. For this very reason, Bṛhan-Manu states: "If a uterine brother is alive, however, a half-brother shall not receive the wealth;
it shall be exactly the same regarding immovable property. In his absence, he (the half-brother) shall indeed receive it. [bM 93]
<11.5.35> "The same would apply even to immovable property" is said with reference to immovable property that has already been partitioned; for immediately thereafter Yama says:
"Whatever immovable property is undivided shall belong to all; immovable property that has been partitioned must never be taken by uterine brothers other than those who share it. [Dhko p. 1561]

<11.5.36> This means "of all [the heirs], whether uterine or non-uterine. Among the uterine brothers alone, if only one is a *saṃsṛṣṭin* (one who has reunited), the inheritance belongs to him alone. When there is both a *saṃsṛṣṭin* uterine brother and a *saṃsṛṣṭin* non-uterine brother, it belongs to both of them. Even when only step-brothers exist, the deceased's wealth should first be understood as belonging to the *saṃsṛṣṭin*; in his absence, it goes to the non-*saṃsṛṣṭin* non-uterine brother.

<11.5.37> For this very reason, the plural form "brothers" (*bhrātaraḥ*) was stated in the aforementioned sequence in order to convey the eligibility of many; otherwise, it would be meaningless. <11.5.38> Furthermore, the rule "the reunited coparcener shall take [the share] of the reunited coparcener" (*saṃsṛṣṭinas tu saṃsṛṣṭī*) is intended to establish a specific distinction based on the association [of inheritance] when there is a gathering of relatives of equal status. <11.5.39> Therefore, whether there exist uterine brothers or half-brothers, or similarly brothers' sons, paternal uncles, and so forth, the one who was reunited shall take [the property] provided they are of equal status, because no distinction is heard in the text. Since all [categories of heirs] are introduced by the preceding statement and since the requirement [for an heir] exists for all of them, the claim that this statement refers exclusively to brothers alone is to be disregarded.
<11.5.40> Thus ends the section on the brother.

Section Six <11.6.1> In his absence, the property goes to the brother’s son. This is because of the statement of Viṣṇu: having declared that "it goes to the brother," he further states, "in his absence, it goes to the brother’s son" (Vi 17.9).

<11.6.2> In this regard, first is the entitlement of the son of a uterine brother; in his absence, the son of a non-uterine brother has the entitlement. This is because of the rule that "the uterine [brother inherits] from the uterine [brother]. For the son of a non-uterine brother, having set aside the mother of the deceased owner, is the giver of the *piṇḍa* to the father of the owner—who is distinguished by being the son of one's own paternal grandfather—and is thus inferior to the son of a uterine brother; consequently, he inherits the wealth immediately after him.

<11.6.3> Nor does there occur an inclusion of the co-wife’s mother, the co-wife’s paternal grandmother, or the co-wife’s paternal great-grandmother in the *śrāddha* by virtue of their being co-wives; for they are included in the *śrāddha* precisely through those same terms. As it is said:
"The mother partakes of the *śrāddha*, consisting of *svadhā*, together with her own husband;
likewise the paternal grandmother and the paternal great-grandmother. [B Śrāddha 75]
Furthermore, the inclusion of co-wives, mothers, and others within the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha is strictly prohibited. As they recite:
"For those who have died without sons—whether women or men—an *ekoddiṣṭa* must be offered for them, not a *pārvaṇa*."

<11.6.4> Furthermore, the rule for the *śrāddha* performed with the wife (*sapatnīka-śrāddha*) is mandatory because it applies to all people; however, the [obligation] regarding the mother and others is non-mandatory. Due to the contradiction between a mandatory and a non-mandatory connection, it is logical that the rule for the *sapatnīka-śrāddha* depends specifically on the mother and others. <11.6.5> [Objection: Just as with the son of a uterine brother, the son of a uterine paternal uncle—because he offers the two ancestral rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) to the deceased father and the previous ancestor (the grandfather) along with their wives—should have an equal entitlement (*adhikāra*) to the wealth as the deceased father’s brother and the son of the paternal uncle.

It is said: for the paternal uncle offers the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) to the two ancestors of the wealth-owner, namely the grandfather and the great-grandfather. However, the brother’s son, taking the wealth-owner’s own father as the primary ancestor, offers the funeral cakes for two generations; thus, he is stronger and is entitled to inherit before the paternal uncle.

For this very reason, even the brother’s grandson supersedes the paternal uncle, because he offers the funeral cakes specifically for the deceased wealth-owner’s own father, who is the primary ancestor.
Even the great-grandson of a brother who possesses wealth is superseded by his paternal uncle, because he falls outside the range of the *piṇḍa* offerings as the fifth descendant. Thus says Manu:
"The water offering is to be made for three; the *piṇḍa* offering extends to three; the fourth is the giver of these, and a fifth does not exist. (MDh 9.186)
By this, the fifth [category of heirs] is excluded.

However, in the absence of even the father’s lineage down to the great-grandson, the entitlement of the father’s daughter’s son (pitṛ-dauhitra) should be understood, just as in the case of the wealth-owner’s daughter’s son. Likewise, the entitlement of the paternal grandfather’s and great-grandfather’s lineages, ending with their respective daughter’s sons, should be understood according to the order of proximity in the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
For the daughter’s son also delivers him in the hereafter, just like a son. [MDh 9.139cd]

For this reason, because there is no distinction, the son of one's father’s sister and others likewise save [the ancestors] by offering the piṇḍas to be consumed by them, just like one's own daughter's son.

<11.6.10> For this very reason, Manu did not show a separate entitlement for these [women], because they are already included by the two statements: "of the three" and "immediately following. And Yājñavalkya used the term *gotraja* (one born of the same lineage) in order to establish the entitlement of even the daughter's son (*dauhitra*) and others born of that lineage, according to the sequence of offering funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*); and in order to exclude women who are *sapiṇḍas*, since they do not belong to that [paternal] lineage. <11.6.11> Therefore, while the phrase "the woman deserves" (*strī... arhati*) continues [from the previous rule], Baudhāyana states: "She does not deserve the inheritance, for women are considered powerless and non-inheritors, according to the Vedic revelation" (Bau 2.2.3.46). The grammatical connection is: "the woman does not deserve the inheritance. However, the entitlement of the wife and others is not contradicted, because of specific scriptural declarations to that effect.

<11.6.12> However, regarding the lineage of the great-grandfather ending with the daughter’s son (*dauhitra*), it is shown by the very statement concerning the immediate sequence of offering rice balls (*piṇḍa*) that—in the absence of one who offers the rice balls to be given to the deceased—the property is for the purpose of offering the three rice balls to the maternal grandfather and others who are to receive them from the deceased.

<11.6.13> Since the three rice balls intended for the maternal grandfather and others who are to receive them from the deceased are offered by the maternal uncle and others, the wealth belongs to the maternal uncle and others; for through the medium of that wealth, they too become the offerers of those rice balls.

For there are two purposes for the acquisition of wealth: for the sake of enjoyment, or for the sake of unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) such as giving. In this case, since the acquirer is deceased, the wealth cannot be enjoyed; therefore, it is logical that it serves only the purpose of unseen merit. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
"From the wealth that has been produced, one should set aside half separately for his [the deceased's] sake."

"One should diligently perform the monthly, six-monthly, and annual *śrāddha* ceremonies. Likewise, Āpastamba states: "A resident pupil (*antevāsī*) or a daughter may employ wealth for those purposes, namely for religious duties (*dharmakṛtya*). The phrase "for religious duties" indicates that the purpose is transcendental (*adṛṣṭa*), as opposed to being for the sake of personal enjoyment; this is the reason given. For this very reason, they recite: "Wealth has its fruit realized through both giving and enjoying.
Therefore, in the absence of one who would otherwise enjoy the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), it is logical that the entitlement belongs to one who must offer that cake, such as a maternal uncle or others.

<11.6.14> Thinking that this very point has already been demonstrated by the two preceding statements, namely "from among these three" and "in the absence of [the previous]," Manu stated immediately thereafter:
"Beyond this, the *sakulya* shall be the heir, or the teacher (*ācārya*), or even the pupil (*śiṣya*).

<11.6.15> A *sakulya* is one belonging to the lineage starting from the great-great-grandfather (*vṛddhaprapitāmaha*) and so forth; they are also called *samanodaka*s. Their right of succession follows the order in which they were mentioned; in their absence, the teacher, the pupil, and others succeed.

<11.6.16> Otherwise, how could the inclusion of maternal uncles and others—which contradicts Manu—be possible? Therefore, there is no contradiction, as this matter was established by Manu himself in the two preceding statements.
<11.6.17> For this very reason, in the section on the division of inheritance, it is said: "Water [libations] are to be offered for three; the *piṇḍa* offering proceeds for three."
"The fourth among these is the recipient; a fifth is not possible.
Having said this, [he continues: "The nearest sapinda and so forth shall be the heir to the property of each respective one. (M 9.186–187ab)

Thus it is written. [The mention of] "the fifth" who is devoid of connection through a single *piṇḍa* is for the purpose of excluding one who lacks the relationship of a single *piṇḍa* with those born in the paternal or maternal lineage, even if such relatives exist. Otherwise, since *sapiṇḍatva* has been declared [in Manu 5.60ab]: "But *sapiṇḍatā* ceases with the seventh person," and since immediate succession (*anantarya*) has been stated by the rule "the one immediately following the *sapiṇḍa*" as the cause for the acquisition of wealth, the word "of three" would be redundant.

Nor should it be said that this is for the purpose of prescribing the *śrāddha* rite for three generations, because it is situated in the middle of the section concerning the division of inheritance. Thus says Manu:

"One should honor the sages with Vedic study, the gods with fire-oblations according to the rule, the ancestors with the *śrāddha*, men with food, and the elemental spirits with the *bali* offering. (MDh 3.81)

Nor should it be said that the statement is intended to establish immediate succession based on the order of birth, rather than immediate succession based on the status of being the giver; for the order of birth is not understood from that statement. Rather, by stating that the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) is to three [ancestors] like water, and that the fourth is the giver of the rice-balls while the fifth is neither the recipient nor the one below—the fifth being the giver of the rice-balls—Manu, in thus declaring immediate succession, makes known that this immediacy is due precisely to the excellence of the status of being the giver.

Therefore, the statement "of three" is intended to establish the eligibility of anyone—whether born of that same family even if not of the same *gotra*, such as one's own daughter's son or father's daughter's son, or someone not born of that family, such as a maternal uncle—who is a *sapiṇḍa* through the connection of a single *piṇḍa* by virtue of being a giver of *piṇḍas* to three generations within the paternal or maternal lineage of the deceased wealth-haver. Furthermore, the term "immediate" (*anantara*) must be explained as being for the purpose of specifying the person who is next in line.

<11.6.20> Therefore, in the absence of those who offer the three funeral cakes (piṇḍas) for the deceased’s father and the other ancestors—such as the paternal daughter’s son (pitṛdauhitra) and others who receive the portion due to the deceased—one should understand that the entitlement belongs, in order of proximity, to those who offer the funeral cakes for the maternal grandfather and others, such as the maternal uncle (mātula) and so forth. <11.6.21> But in the absence of anyone up to this point, a distant kinsman (sakulya) is entitled. Regarding this, Manu says: "In his absence, a distant kinsman (sakulya) shall be the heir, or a teacher (ācārya), or even a pupil (śiṣya). [M 9.187cd]

A *sakulya* (a kinsman of the same lineage) consists of three generations descending from the great-grandson (*pratipraṇaptṛ*)—those who have received separate funeral cakes (*vibhaktapiṇḍa*)—as well as the line of descendants beginning with the great-great-grandfather.

Even among these, the immediate proximity of the great-grandson and the others is due to their being benefactors by means of receiving the remnants of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍalepa*). In their absence, the line of descendants beginning with the great-great-grandfather [is included], because they are the givers of the funeral cakes to the great-great-grandfather and others who consume the remnants of the cakes offered to the deceased.
In the absence of such *sakulyas*, the *samānodakas* (distant kinsmen) are to be understood as being included by the very term *sakulya*.

In their absence, the teacher (*ācārya*); in his absence as well, the pupil (*śiṣya*), according to the statement of Manu: "The teacher or even the pupil. In their absence, a fellow student (*sabrahmacārī*), based on the designation: "The pupil [is the heir] of the fellow student. In their absence, those of the same *gotra*; and in their absence, those of the same *pravara*, according to the statement of Gautama: "Those related by the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), the *gotra*, or the *ṛṣi* shall divide the inheritance."
<11.6.26> But in the absence of all those mentioned above, Brāhmaṇas shall take that wealth. Regarding this, Manu says:
"In the absence of all [others], however, Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the three Vedas, pure, and self-controlled, shall be the sharers of the inheritance; thus the Dharma is not violated. [M 9.188]

Even though his merit (*dharma*) is being diminished by the enjoyment [of his property], it does not perish because it is replenished by the acquisition of another merit through the fact that his wealth goes to Brāhmaṇas; thus, in this case as well, he prioritizes the fact that the wealth is intended for that very purpose.
In the absence of such [Brāhmaṇas], the king should take [the property], excluding the wealth of Brāhmaṇas.

This absence of Brāhmaṇas related to the *gotra* and the *ṛṣi* lineage should be understood as occurring within that village; otherwise, the king’s jurisdiction would result in being rendered without an object.

In this regard, if the entitlement of the father’s daughter’s son, the maternal uncle, and others had not been stated by the verse beginning with "of the three" (*tatra yadi trayāṇām*), then, because there would be no place for them among the *sakulyas* and others who follow a fixed order of succession, they would have no entitlement at all. Nor can it be said that let them have no entitlement; for Yājñavalkya has indicated their existence through the terms *gotraja* and *bandhu*. Therefore, it must be admitted that Manu has also indicated them by the very phrase "of the three."
Therefore, the order of entitlement should be followed in such a way that the deceased’s wealth becomes most beneficial to him.

For this very reason, the equal entitlement of the son, grandson, and great-grandson is established; for from such scriptural statements as "By means of a son one conquers the worlds," an equal benefit is heard, and there is no distinction in the offering of the funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) to them.

For this very reason, it is established that there is no entitlement for a grandson or a great-grandson whose father is living. This is because the Vedic injunction, "One should not offer across a living person," prohibits those two from performing the *pārvaṇa* rite by bypassing their living father, as they would otherwise fail to benefit him. Otherwise, such an entitlement would apply even to those two whose fathers are deceased. Furthermore, if the order were determined by the sequence of birth, the entitlement would belong to the son alone due to his immediate proximity (*sapiṇḍānantarya*) to the ancestor, and not to the grandson or the great-grandson. Moreover, there exists no scriptural statement that establishes the simultaneous entitlement of these three—the son and the others—concurrently.

Therefore, precisely because there is no difference in the benefit conferred, the connection to the wealth must be stated as being equal. <11.6.30> In this way, according to the method previously stated, it should be understood that the wealth of the deceased belongs for the sake of the deceased, following the sequence already mentioned.

<11.6.31> And this very point is established because, in the section on inheritance (*dāyabhāga*), the statement regarding the sons and others' superior capacity to confer benefit has no other purpose; for it is said: "And he who has indeed discharged his debts to the ancestors, therefore he deserves to receive [the inheritance]. [M 9.106cd]
Because the discharge of debt is proclaimed as a cause for the acquisition of wealth;

and because, by the verse "For even through a daughter’s son he rescues him in the next world, just like a son’s son," the act of rescuing is likewise indicated as being caused by a connection with wealth.

Furthermore, because there is no other basis for a connection to wealth equal to that of the three—sons and the rest—and because [the rule] stating "water for the three" and so forth would otherwise result in redundancy; because eunuchs, outcasts, those born blind, and others are excluded from inheritance precisely because they provide no benefit; because it would involve the excessive complexity of postulating a scriptural injunction to grant rights to relatives; and because it is only logical that wealth acquired by them should be made available to them in proportion to the degree of their benefit.
It is understood that the connection with wealth for Manu and others is rightly established solely on the basis of their being benefactors;
this point, illuminated by the light of faultless knowledge, should be respected by the learned.

Even if there were dissatisfaction among the wise regarding this, and [it were argued] that this matter is merely based on the literal text (*vācanika*), nevertheless, let it be that the meaning of the two statements is to be accepted exactly as stated. What is the use of further elaboration?

<11.6.34> The king shall take [the property], with the exception of the wealth of a Brāhmaṇa. Regarding this, Manu says: "The property of a Brāhmaṇa must never be seized by the king; such is the established rule. However, in the absence of all [other heirs], the king may take the property of the other castes. [M 9.189]
By the word "all," the inclusion extends down to the Brāhmaṇas.

The wealth of forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*), ascetics (*yati*), and students (*brahmacārin*) shall be taken by their spiritual brothers (*dharmabhrātṛ*), virtuous disciples, and teachers (*ācārya*). In their absence, one belonging to the same religious order (*ekatīrthya*) or the same stage of life (*ekāśramin*) shall take it. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"The heirs of the forest-dwellers, ascetics, and students [are their spiritual brothers, etc.]."

The wealth [of the deceased] should be understood to belong, respectively, to the teacher (*ācārya*), the virtuous disciple (*sacchiṣya*), the spiritual brother (*dharmabhrātṛ*), and those who share the same sacred ford (*ekatīrthin*), according to the inverse order (*pratilomakrama*) as far as applicable. Furthermore, the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārī*) is intended here; for he has fulfilled his obligation by residing in and serving the teacher’s household for the rest of his life, having renounced his father and others. However, the wealth of the student who returns home (*upakurvāṇa*) must be taken by the father and the other relatives themselves.
<11.6.37> Thus concludes the section on the right to the estate of those who have no sons and so forth.
CHAPTER TWELVE <12.1> Now follows the division of reunited property. Regarding this, Manu and Viṣṇu state:

"If those who were previously divided should reunite and live together, their division [upon re-separation] shall be equal; in that case, the status of primogeniture does not exist. (M 9.210 = Vi 18.41) The phrase "in that case" (*tatra*) refers to the case of brothers of the same caste (*savarṇa*) reuniting. However, in the case of a union between a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya, the arrangement of shares must be understood as following the proportions already determined previously. For the statement regarding equality is intended solely to prohibit the previously ordained special share for the eldest. Therefore, Bṛhaspati says:
"But for brothers who have already divided and then live together again out of affection, there is no seniority (*jyaiṣṭhya*) in the event of a subsequent division.
This [verse] prohibits only the additional share due to seniority, but it does not teach that the shares must be equal.
<12.3> Furthermore, those who are reunited are described by Bṛhaspati:
"He who, having been divided from his father or brother, again dwells together with them in one place, or with his paternal uncle out of affection, is called 'reunited' (saṃsṛṣṭa). [B 26.113]

<12.4> Thus, regarding those cases excluded from the enumeration, a distinction based on association is not to be respected, as it would render the enumeration purposeless. <12.5> Other distinctions, however, should be followed as stated in the section defining the authority of brothers. <12.6> Thus ends the division of property among those who have reunited.
CHAPTER THIRTEEN.

<13.1> Now, regarding the division of property that was concealed at the time of partition and discovered afterwards: on this point, Manu says: "When all debts and assets have been divided according to rule, whatever is subsequently discovered, all of that should be brought into equality. [M 9.218]

<13.2> Just as the allotment of shares was previously made for each person, it must be done in exactly that same manner. The meaning of the word "equally" (*samatām nayet*) is that one should not give a smaller share to the appropriator simply because he is an appropriator, nor should one not give him any at all; rather, one should bring about equality. However, this statement does not mean that everyone should receive equal shares of that property, because there would be no reason to set aside the "twenty-part deduction" (*viṃśoddhāra*) and other such rules, and because it would result in Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and others receiving equal shares. <13.3> Likewise, Yājñavalkya says: "Where property stolen from one another is seen among those who have already divided [their inheritance]..."
Furthermore, they should divide that again into equal shares; this is the settled rule.
Likewise, Kātyāyana says:
"But whatever has been concealed by someone, upon returning, that shall be divided equally."

Sons should divide [the estate] together with their brothers even in the absence of the father. Whatever property may have been withheld from one another or improperly divided, and which is subsequently discovered, that shall be divided into equal shares; so says Bhṛgu.

<13.5> He further demonstrates the division of that which was not previously divided: "The share falls once" refers to the subject of a correct division. <13.6> "Obtained afterwards" means that even what was previously divided need not be divided again. <13.7> Likewise, Kātyāyana says:
"One must never cause property seized by a relative to be returned by force;
one must never cause the enjoyment of undivided relatives to be surrendered. [K 888]

He should be made to pay by means of conciliation and other such methods, but not by force. Furthermore, that which was enjoyed in excess by one who was undivided [from the family] need not be paid by him.

Regarding this, for those who think that since there is "another's property" even within common property, one becomes a thief and incurs guilt by concealing it, it is said in reply: It is a matter of worldly convention that he alone is called a thief who, knowing specifically that "this belongs to another," falsely attributes ownership to another's property despite the absence of any cause for such ownership. And in this case, one is unable to distinguish whether "this belongs to another" or "this is mine," because the property is undivided.

Just as the completion of a gift occurs only when the owner relinquishes a specific object with the thought "this is mine" for the sake of transferring it to another's ownership, and the other person specifically recognizes it as their own with the thought "this is mine," such a process is not possible in the case of communal property; therefore, communal property is said to be ungivable. Likewise, theft also occurs only for one who knows "this is not my wealth, but this belongs to another"; thus, the completion of theft does not occur through the misappropriation of communal property.

The term *aparārpaṇa* (non-delivery), however, is intended to mean concealment. Yet, concealment alone does not constitute theft, for we observe the application of the term "theft" even in cases where there is taking of another's property without concealment. Thus Kātyāyana says:
Whether secretly or openly, by night or by day, the taking of another's property is proclaimed to be theft. [K 810]

For this very reason, it was stated previously that the king should not force [the thief] to pay by means of physical compulsion. However, in the case of actual theft, according to the scriptural injunction: "The king, having made the thief restore what was stolen, should have him executed by various forms of capital punishment" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.270ab), let alone making him pay through conciliation (*sāman*) and other means, even execution must be carried out.

<13.10> And this is inferred by the sages even from the case of one who takes [the property], because of the subsequent division, giving, and restitution. <13.11> This has also been stated by Viśvarūpa: "Therefore, there is no fault of theft, because of the force of the commencement of the verbal expression; the intention is that the meaning of the verbal root *steya* (to steal) is not accomplished."

For this very reason, it was stated by Jitendriya in the *Prāyaścittakāṇḍa*: "If one takes what belongs to another gold, thinking it to be iron or the like; or if one takes what is not gold, thinking it to be gold; or if one takes what belongs to another, thinking it to be one's own—similar to what is already one's own—in all these cases there is no completion of theft (*apahāra*). This is because in every instance, there is an absence of the cognition that the object belongs to another, corresponding to the actual state of things. The same applies here [in the case of the division of the inheritance]: prior to the division, there is no recognition of the ownership residing in a specific portion manifested by that [act of division]. Therefore, there is no completion of theft here."

Alternatively, even if theft were present, there would be no fault of theft because we observe scriptural statements regarding the partitioning of the property even for the one who has stolen it; otherwise, there would be no share for one who is an outcast (*patita*) due to the concealment of gold and other such items. If it is argued that, although the theft of gold—which is a cause for a grave sin—is a ground for exclusion, the rule for partition is explained as referring to the theft of other types of property because there is no specific statement to the contrary regarding the thief’s share in the case of gold, [we reply: if that is so, why is the prohibition against stealing gold and the like not established as applying exclusively to property belonging to others that is not common [to all]? If you ask what the decisive evidence (*vinigamanā-pramāṇa*) is for this, [the answer follows].

It is said: theft (*steya*) is the taking of another’s property; since the word "another" (*para*) excludes one's own ownership, it implies the state of being owned by another. Furthermore, between a common and a specific [meaning], the specific is more swiftly understood. Just as in the case of the statement, "This *paurṇamāsa* oblation is preceded by [the wish] as one desires," the displacement (*utkarṣa*) applies only to the *agnīṣomīya* sacrificial cake and not to the *upāṃśuyāja*, because the latter belongs in common to both Agni and Soma. For this very reason, even in worldly usage, no such process of determination or the like is observed in similar cases.

Therefore, that which is the speech of a child—namely, that just as when there is a substitution of *māṣa* beans for *mudga* beans in the event of a shortage of *mudgas*, and while both are connected to the sacrifice, the *māṣas* are prohibited by the rule "beans (*māṣas*) are indeed unfit for sacrifice," so too in the case of taking what belongs to oneself, the theft of what does not belong to oneself is prohibited—that is merely the speech of a child. This is because the very category of "theft" (*steya*) as previously defined is absent here. For it cannot be said that the *māṣa* beans have no connection to the sacrifice when the constituent parts of the *mudga* beans are being taken from them; rather, it is precisely those [beans] mixed with *māṣas* that are perceived as having a connection to the sacrifice.
<13.17> Thus ends the section on the mutual removal of distinctions.
CHAPTER FOURTEEN <14.1> Now follows the determination of doubts regarding the division of meters (*vṛtta*). On this matter, Nārada says:

When there is doubt regarding the law of partition among heirs, the decision is made by the kinsmen (*jñāti*) through a collective division, because they carry out the affairs separately. (N 13.36) <14.2> The mention of "kinsmen" is for the purpose of indicating that while they are present, no other witnesses are to be taken; for this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:

When there is a denial of partition, the proof of partition is to be known through kinsmen, relatives, witnesses, documents, and separate properties consisting of houses and fields. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.149) First, the *jñātis*—the *sapiṇḍas*—are the witnesses. In their absence, the *bandhus*, that is, the connected relatives who have been brought forward, are the witnesses. In their absence, even neutral persons (*udāsīna*) may be witnesses; for if they were equally eligible, they would already have been included by the term "witness" itself, which would render the terms *jñāti* and *bandhu* redundant. For this very reason, Śaṅkha says:

When a doubt arises regarding the distinction between the lineage portion (*gotrabhāga*) and the non-lineage portion, and the members of the lineage (*gotraja*) themselves do not know [the matter], a member of the family (*kula*) is worthy of being a witness. "Members of the lineage" means kinsmen (*jñāti*); when they do not know [it], a relative (*bandhu*) is worthy of being a witness, but not one who is unrelated. When even he does not know it, another person is the witness; such is the meaning.

<14.5> For this very reason, Nārada has specified that kinsmen (*jñāti*) alone are the primary [means of proof]. The reading *jñātṛbhiḥ* (by those who know) is not based on an authoritative source. <14.6> Likewise, a decision may be reached through written evidence (*likhita*). It has been stated that written evidence is indeed more powerful than witnesses. <14.7> Furthermore, a decision may be reached from the separate conduct of the case; as it was said by Nārada:

The acceptance of gifts, the ownership of livestock, food, houses, and fields, as well as cooking, religious duties, income, and expenditures, are to be understood as distinct for those who have divided their property.
Likewise, the roles of witness, suretyship, giving, and receiving are also distinct.
Brothers who have divided their inheritance may perform legal acts for one another, but not those who have not divided;
for those among whom these transactions proceed in the world according to their own property rights,
one should understand them to be divided even in the absence of a written document.

Likewise, Bṛhaspati says: "In cases of violence, immovable property, a deposit, and the prior partition of inheritance among heirs, the matter is to be known through inference; in these instances, neither documents nor witnesses are admissible. [B 26.143]
The obstruction of the continuity of power, secret theft involving acts of violence, the enjoyment of one's own immovable property, separate wealth from the partition,
separate income, expenditure, and assets, and mutual lending at interest.
And those who establish trade routes shall undoubtedly be divided [among themselves].

<14.9> One brother gives, and the other receives; the household and so forth, as well as the state of income and expenditure, are separate for each. When one engages in debts and such matters, the other is made a witness or a guarantor; or there is a mutual transaction involving debts and the like. One buys some property from another and sells it to his brother for the purpose of trade. Such individual actions as these are possible only among those who are mutually divided. By means of such [actions], the learned should infer the partition.

<14.10> Nor should it be asserted that because these actions belong to those [who are not witnesses], the word "these" (*etāḥ*)—by virtue of referring to many—indicates only those who are tainted; for statements are rooted in logic (*nyāya*), and since the logic applies without distinction to each individual case as well. <14.11> By the statement "there would be neither documents nor witnesses," it is said that in the absence of documents and witnesses, one must resort to inference (*anumāna*).
Chapter Fifteen.
It is not possible here to please the people by awakening their understanding of the true nature of inheritance, which has been obstructed by reverence for the Teacher;
rather, the effort of the learned is made solely to provide a point of agreement with those sages whose intellects are dependent upon valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
This treatise composed by Jīmūtavāhana should be contemplated for the removal of the doubts arising from the various commentaries of earlier authors.
Thus ends the section on the Partition of Inheritance in the *Dharmaratna* composed by the great preceptor Śrī Jīmūtavāhana of the Pāribhadra lineage.
